Sheet 1 / 11 · Unit 12a–12b · Nature

Aims of the lesson & Lead-in

Aims of the lesson

After these four periods, you should be able to:

📚Remember · Understand
  • Name the words and chunks of the 4 groups: extreme weather, “What if …?” science, natural and man-made places, wildlife and nature photography.
  • Explain how the second conditional is built and why it describes unlikely or imagined situations, not real plans.
  • Recognise what every-, some-, no-, any- and -one, -body, -thing, -where add to words like nobody and somewhere.
🛠️Apply · Analyse
  • Use the second conditional to imagine wild weather, hopes and dreams: If I …, I’d … · What would you do if …?
  • Choose between everyone, something, nowhere, anything … in statements, negatives and questions.
  • Find facts, reasons and opinions in the article What if …?, the documentary about David Liittschwager and the PET Reading and Listening extras.
💡Evaluate · Create
  • Describe and evaluate, with the 7-step frame, a storm or flood you know about (Topic 7) or a wild animal you have seen (Topic 8).
  • Write one cause–effect paragraph, frame by frame, imagining city life without any green spaces.
  • Value the nature close to you with curiosity, and share ideas respectfully in pair and group work.

Lead-in 1 · Storms, ice and a green cube: look, guess and react

4:00Pick a photo for your partner, listen to their three answers, then swap.
Too close to a tornado?
  1. Question 1
    ‘Describe what you can see: the sky, the land, the car and the funnel.’
  2. Question 2
    ‘Read the words on the back of the car. Who is inside, and why have they stopped so close?’
  3. Question 3
    ‘If you were in the passenger seat right now, what would you say to the driver?’
Model answer

The sky is half blue and half dark grey, and a column of brown dust is whirling over completely flat fields. The car says ‘Severe Weather Research Unit’, so I’d guess the people inside are scientists who want to measure the storm. If I were the passenger, I’d be shouting at the driver to turn the car round!

A motorway in a snowstorm
  1. Question 1
    ‘How far ahead can these drivers see, do you think? Why have they all switched their lights on?’
  2. Question 2
    ‘Which part of the world could this be? What do the bare trees tell you about the season?’
  3. Question 3
    ‘Would you rather drive through heavy snow or through a flooded street? Why?’
Model answer

I doubt they can see more than fifty metres, so the lights are there to help other drivers spot them. With no leaves on the trees, it must be the middle of winter, somewhere like northern Europe. I’d take the snow, because in a flood you have no idea how deep the water is.

Only the roofs are dry
  1. Question 1
    ‘How deep is the water? Use the cars to measure it.’
  2. Question 2
    ‘What do you think happened in the hours before this photo was taken?’
  3. Question 3
    ‘If you were sent to help in this town, which health problems would you expect over the next week?’
Model answer

The water reaches the tops of the cars, so it’s probably about one and a half metres deep. My guess is that it rained hard all night and the river burst its banks before dawn. I’d expect skin infections, stomach bugs from dirty water, and plenty of older people who have run out of their regular medicine.

A city lit up from above
  1. Question 1
    ‘Count the bolts of lightning. Where do you think they are hitting?’
  2. Question 2
    ‘We see the flash before we hear the thunder. Why do you think that is?’
  3. Question 3
    ‘Do storms like this frighten you, or do you enjoy watching them from a window?’
Model answer

I can count at least three bolts, and they seem to be hitting the edge of the city, maybe a tower or a hill. Light travels much faster than sound, so the flash reaches us first and the thunder follows a few seconds later. I actually love a good storm, as long as I’m indoors with the windows shut.

A handful of ice
  1. Question 1
    ‘What are these white balls, and where did they fall from?’
  2. Question 2
    ‘Compare their size with something you know: a grape, an egg or a ping-pong ball?’
  3. Question 3
    ‘What could a storm of stones this size do to a roof, a car or a field of young rice?’
Model answer

They’re hailstones, and they must have come down from a storm cloud only minutes ago, before they had time to melt. Most are about as big as a large grape, and a couple are nearly the size of a ping-pong ball. Hail like this could crack roof tiles and flatten a whole rice field in a few minutes.

Above the waves or below them?
  1. Question 1
    ‘Look at the two people in the boat and the submarine under them. Who is in more danger?’
  2. Question 2
    ‘This painting comes from a science blog. What do you think a reader asked the scientist?’
  3. Question 3
    ‘Make up your own strange weather question that starts with What if … and ask your partner.’
Model answer

The two people in the boat, no question. They’re sitting up on a flat sea, and the submarine is hiding deep under the water. I think the reader wanted to know whether you’d be safe under the sea in a storm. Here’s mine: what if it rained for a whole year and never stopped?

A green frame on fallen leaves
  1. Question 1
    ‘What do you think this green metal frame is for?’
  2. Question 2
    ‘Is this a wild forest far from any town, or could it be a park in a huge city? What makes you think so?’
  3. Question 3
    ‘How many different living things do you think you could find inside it in one afternoon?’
Model answer

It looks like a tool for measuring, as if someone wants to study exactly one small piece of ground. The trees look wild, but the ground under them is quite open and tidy, so I’d guess it’s a big city park. If I really looked closely, I bet I’d find twenty or thirty kinds of insects, worms and tiny plants.

The same frame under the sea
  1. Question 1
    ‘What lives inside this cube? Name everything you can see.’
  2. Question 2
    ‘Why would a photographer carry the same frame to the sea, a forest and a city park?’
  3. Question 3
    ‘Would you rather photograph wildlife under the sea or on a mountain top? Why?’
Model answer

There’s a striped fish, some pink and orange coral and lots of tiny plants growing on the rocks. Using one frame everywhere makes the photos easy to compare, because each place gets exactly the same amount of space. I’d go for the sea, even though I’m a terrible swimmer, because nothing on land is that colourful.

Lead-in 2 · Weather, dreams and nature: agree or disagree?

4:00Tap your side, then back it up with a reason and something you have seen yourself.

1 · Extreme weather happens more often now than when our grandparents were young.

Model answer

I’d agree. My grandmother’s village in central Vietnam used to flood once every ten years or so, and now the water comes up most autumns. Summers in Hà Nội seem to start earlier every year, too.

2 · Storm chasers take risks that nobody should take.

Model answer

Not completely. The scientists among them collect data that helps forecasters send out warnings earlier, so their risk can save lives. The people who only want a dramatic video for social media, though? I can’t see the point.

3 · If I had a free year, I’d spend it travelling, not studying.

Model answer

Definitely travelling. I’ve been studying non-stop since I was six, and I’d love to ride a motorbike from the Chinese border all the way down to Cà Mau Cape. I’d probably pack a couple of medical books, though, just in case.

4 · Strange “What if …?” questions are a good way to learn science.

Model answer

I agree, because a funny question makes you want the answer. A friend sent me a two-minute video about what would happen if you fell into a black hole, and I ended up reading about black holes until two in the morning. No textbook chapter has ever kept me up that late.

5 · You don’t need to leave the city to find nature.

Model answer

That’s true, you just have to slow down. The old trees behind our lecture hall fill up with noisy birds every evening, and I once counted four kinds of butterfly in the flower bed by the canteen.

6 · A beautiful photo of nature can make people want to protect it.

Model answer

Partly. A photo of a sea turtle caught in a plastic bag made me stop buying bottled water for a whole month. But a month isn’t very long, so I think a photo starts the feeling and the law has to do the rest.

Useful language
  • I’d say that’s true, especially when …
  • In my experience, …
  • It depends on …, to be honest.
  • I see your point, but …
  • I’m not convinced, because …

Lead-in 3 · Listen · Track 93 · Storm chasers

6:00Read the five questions, listen twice, then talk about SB Ex 3 with a partner.
Track 93

Listen to part of a documentary about storm chasers and choose the best answer (SB p. 141 Ex 2)

Played 0×
Transcript · Audioscript 93

When a tornado is coming, most people drive in the opposite direction. But storm chasers look for tornadoes and drive towards them. Some storm chasers are scientists and they try to learn more about how tornadoes are formed. Other storm chasers are just everyday people who are interested and want to get good photos. The most common time of day to see a tornado is between 4 p.m. and 9 p.m., but they can be very unpredictable. They can change direction at any moment and so they are difficult to follow. That also makes them extremely dangerous. They can destroy trees and houses in seconds and some storm chasers have died while they were following tornadoes.

1According to the speaker, what makes storm chasers different from most people?
The speaker sets the two groups against each other: “most people drive in the opposite direction. But storm chasers … drive towards them.” Going towards what others run from = D. Option C borrows the words opposite direction, but that is what ordinary drivers do, and nobody tells them to.
2Which sentence best explains the difference between the two kinds of storm chaser?
“Some … are scientists and they try to learn more about how tornadoes are formed” = they want to understand how tornadoes form. “Other storm chasers are just everyday people who are interested and want to get good photos” = curious people who want pictures. D swaps the two groups round; B is wrong because both groups drive towards the storm.
3A storm chaser has one free day in tornado season. When does she have the best chance of seeing a tornado?
“The most common time of day to see a tornado is between 4 p.m. and 9 p.m.” = the late afternoon and early evening. Most common tells you that some tornadoes come at other hours, so D (equally often all day) is wrong, and E starts exactly where the window ends.
4‘That also makes them extremely dangerous.’ What does That refer to?
That points back to the sentence just before it: tornadoes “can change direction at any moment and so they are difficult to follow.” A storm that can turn without warning may suddenly come straight at the people following it. E is mentioned only after That, as the result of the danger.
5Why does the speaker end with the fact that some storm chasers have died?
The last sentence, “some storm chasers have died while they were following tornadoes”, states a fact that shows how serious the danger is. The speaker never says the hobby should be stopped (A goes too far), and nothing in the recording compares the driving of the two groups (F).
SB p. 141 Ex 3 · Think, then tell the class
  1. Why do you think people want to be storm chasers?
  2. Would you like to be a storm chaser? Why? / Why not?
Model answer · question 1

Some of them are scientists who need measurements from right next to the storm, and there’s no other way to get them. For everyone else, I think it’s the thrill. Standing that close to something so powerful must make you feel tiny and very alive at the same time.

Model answer · question 2

Honestly, no. I’d love to see a tornado once in my life, but from a long way off with a good zoom lens. I’d rather spend my energy treating the people a storm has hurt than driving after the storm itself.

Useful language
  • I think people do it because …
  • It must feel … to stand so close to …
  • I’d love to …, but only if …
  • There’s no way I’d …, because …

Sheet 2 / 11 · Unit 12a–12b · 4 periods

Roadmap

Learning outcomes

Reading · SB p. 142 + PET Parts 2–4
  • What if …? (listen and read, Track 94) and three PET texts
  • Scientific reasons, reference words, inference and the writer’s purpose
  • 7 out of 10 or more in Reading A and in each PET part
Listening · Tracks 95–96 + PET Parts 1, 3, 4
  • Listening A: two people imagine a hotter climate (would · wouldn’t · ’d)
  • Listening B: the documentary about David Liittschwager’s green cube
  • PET: seven short extracts, a guide’s talk at Cúc Phương National Park, a radio interview with a young doctor
  • 7 out of 10 or more in Listening A, Listening B and each PET part
Speaking · Parts 1–3
  • Part 1: Point → Why → Example, with one chunk from Sheet 4
  • Part 2: two minutes on card A (Topic 7, extreme weather) or card B (Topic 8, a wild animal)
  • Part 3: a one-minute answer that walks through the whole 7-step frame
  • Sheet 11: a 20-second “What if …?” answer, then a tiny patch of nature close to where you live
Writing · the cause–effect paragraph
  • A single paragraph: 8–10 sentences, 140–170 words
  • A topic sentence that tells the reader to expect causes or effects
  • Each cause or effect explained as a chain (because → so / as a result) and backed by one specific example
  • A closing sentence that sums up and adds nothing new
  • Frame C puts would in every effect, every result and the closing sentence
Grammar
  • The second conditional: past simple after if, would + verb in the other clause, a comma only when if comes first
  • every- / some- / no- / any- + -one / -body / -thing / -where: the right word, a singular verb, no double negative
  • 8 out of 10 or more in Exercises 7–15
Vocabulary
  • Chunks from all four groups in your spoken answers and your paragraph
  • The Sheet 10 quiz a week later: at least 13 of the 16 chunks
  • 8 out of 10 or more in Exercises 1–6

How to learn a group of words

1

Read the Core aloud

  • Start with the words you already listed in Lead-in 4
  • Read each example twice: slowly, then at normal speed
2

Choose 5 Advanced words

  • The five you would need to describe a typhoon or a national park
  • Leave the others for next week
3

Hide and recall

  • Hide the meaning line and explain the word in English
  • Hide the word and get it back from its meaning
4

Write one true sentence

  • About the weather where you grew up, or a wild place you love
  • Use two new chunks and the pattern If …, I’d …
5

Talk for 30 seconds

  • Say your sentence and add two more, using one every- / some- / no- / any- word
  • Start with If I could go anywhere, …
Sheet 3 / 11 · 4 vocabulary groups · What if …? & Nature in one cubic foot

Vocabulary: extreme weather, imagined situations, places and wildlife

Group 1 · Extreme weather — storms, floods and hail

Core
Weather words
a flood / flood (v) /flʌd/
water that rises and spreads over streets, fields or homes · (v) cover a place with water
The flood last October cut the road to our training area for a week, and the rice fields beside it still flood after every big storm.
hail /heɪl/
frozen raindrops that come down as small, hard lumps of ice
Hail the size of peanuts bounced off the roof of the field kitchen for ten noisy minutes.
a snowstorm /ˈsnəʊstɔːm/
a time when a lot of snow falls, often blown by strong winds
On the exchange trip to Russia, a snowstorm kept our group inside the hostel for two whole days.
thunder /ˈθʌndə(r)/
the deep, rolling boom that follows a flash in a stormy sky
A single crash of thunder woke half the ward at three in the morning.
lightning /ˈlaɪtnɪŋ/
the sudden flash of bright light in the sky during a storm, caused by electricity
We counted the seconds between the lightning and the crash that followed to guess how far away the storm was.
a thunderstorm /ˈθʌndəstɔːm/
a period of heavy rain with loud bangs and flashes of light in the sky
A thunderstorm knocked out the power during our evening shift, and the ward sat in the dark until the backup lights flickered on.
a tornado /tɔːˈneɪdəʊ/
a violent, twisting wind shaped like a funnel that travels over the ground
From the car window, the tornado looked like a grey rope hanging down from the clouds.
a storm /stɔːm/
a time of very bad weather with strong winds and usually rain
The storm knocked down two trees by the academy gate, and our company spent Sunday morning clearing the branches.
freezing /ˈfriːzɪŋ/
extremely cold; below zero degrees Celsius
It was freezing on the night march in the hills, and by midnight nobody could feel their fingers.
heavy rain /ˌhevi ˈreɪn/
a lot of water falling from the clouds in a short time
Heavy rain turned the path to the field hospital into thick red mud.
Danger and safety
a storm chaser /ˈstɔːm tʃeɪsə(r)/
a person who follows violent weather to study it or to film it
A storm chaser needs a fast car, a good map and the sense to turn back when the wind changes.
chase /tʃeɪs/
run or drive after someone or something to catch it or keep it in sight
Two cadets chased a runaway dog across the parade ground while the whole platoon laughed.
destroy /dɪˈstrɔɪ/
damage something so badly that it cannot be used or repaired
The landslide destroyed the only bridge to the village, so the medical team walked the last five kilometres.
unpredictable /ˌʌnprɪˈdɪktəbl/
changing so often or so fast that you never know what comes next
Mountain weather is unpredictable: a sunny morning can turn into a cold, wet afternoon in under an hour.
dangerous /ˈdeɪndʒərəs/
able to cause harm, injury or death
Driving across a flooded road is dangerous, because fast-moving water can push even a heavy truck sideways.
safe /seɪf/
protected from harm; not likely to be hurt
The nurses moved the oldest patients to the top floor, where they would be safe if the water kept rising.
a weather forecast /ˈweðə fɔːkɑːst/
a report on TV, radio or online that says what the sky and temperature will be like soon
The weather forecast promised a dry weekend, so the platoon leader planned the river crossing for Saturday.
a warning /ˈwɔːnɪŋ/
a message that tells people about a danger before it arrives
The commune loudspeakers gave a warning at six in the morning, and by noon every fishing boat was tied up in the harbour.
damage /ˈdæmɪdʒ/
physical harm that leaves something broken, weaker or less useful
Engineers came to check the damage to the clinic roof the morning after the typhoon.
Advanced
Disasters and what people do
a typhoon/taɪˈfuːn/the name used in the western Pacific and the East Sea for a hurricane: a huge spinning storm that forms over warm seaIn autumn, the central provinces often have to prepare for a typhoon coming in from the East Sea.
a heatwave/ˈhiːtweɪv/several days of unusually hot weatherDuring the June heatwave, the academy moved morning exercise to five o'clock to avoid the worst of the sun.
a drought/draʊt/a long dry spell, when the ground cracks and crops and animals are short of waterAfter months of drought, the village wells were empty and the clinic had its water brought in by truck.
a landslide/ˈlændslaɪd/a mass of earth, mud and rocks that suddenly falls down a steep slopeA week of rain caused a landslide that blocked the road to the border post, so supplies came in by helicopter.
a flash flood/ˌflæʃ ˈflʌd/a sudden rush of water after very heavy rain, which comes and goes quicklyA flash flood can fill a dry stream bed in minutes, so never pitch your tent right next to one.
evacuate/ɪˈvækjueɪt/get people out of an area in danger and take them to a safer oneBefore the storm arrived, soldiers helped evacuate about two hundred families from the coastal villages.
Collocations
Talking about storms and their dangers
be hit by lightning/bi ˌhɪt baɪ ˈlaɪtnɪŋ/be struck by an electric flash from the skyThe old banyan tree in the yard was hit by lightning last summer, and half of it turned black.
a flood warning/ˈflʌd wɔːnɪŋ/an official message that rivers may rise and cover the landAs soon as the flood warning came, the hospital moved its medicines and oxygen tanks upstairs.
check the weather forecast/ˌtʃek ðə ˈweðə fɔːkɑːst/look up what conditions are expected over the next few daysAlways check the weather forecast before a trek: a dry path today can be a stream tomorrow.
cause serious damage/ˌkɔːz ˌsɪəriəs ˈdæmɪdʒ/harm buildings, roads or crops very badlyStrong winds can cause serious damage to field tents, so we tie them down with extra ropes.
drive in the opposite direction/ˌdraɪv ɪn ði ˌɒpəzɪt dəˈrekʃn/go by car away from something, not towards itIf the road ahead is under water, turn round and drive in the opposite direction, even if it adds an hour to the trip.
freezing temperatures/ˌfriːzɪŋ ˈtemprətʃəz/weather so cold that water turns to iceThe water pipes at the mountain clinic burst after three nights of freezing temperatures.

Group 2 · What if …? — science answers and imagined situations

Core
The science
a submarine /ˌsʌbməˈriːn/
a ship that can dive and travel deep in the sea
Doctors who serve on a submarine may not see daylight for weeks at a time.
underwater /ˌʌndəˈwɔːtə(r)/
below the surface of the sea, a river or a lake
We practised underwater rescue in the academy pool, holding our breath for thirty seconds at a time.
a flat surface /ˌflæt ˈsɜːfɪs/
a level area with no bumps, holes or high points
For chest compressions, the patient must lie on a firm, flat surface, not a soft mattress.
electrical energy /ɪˌlektrɪkl ˈenədʒi/
the power carried by electricity, like the power in a battery or a lightning bolt
A defibrillator sends a short burst of electrical energy through the heart to bring back a normal rhythm.
spread (outwards) /spred/ · /ˈaʊtwədz/
grow or move out from the middle towards all sides
Redness that spreads outwards from a small cut can be an early sign of infection.
the speed of sound /ðə ˌspiːd əv ˈsaʊnd/
how fast noise travels through the air: about 1,200 km an hour
Some fighter jets fly faster than the speed of sound, and the bang you hear on the ground comes after the plane has passed.
a windscreen /ˈwɪndskriːn/
the large glass window at the front of a car or truck
A stone flew up and hit the ambulance's windscreen on the mountain road, leaving a long crack.
take off /ˌteɪk ˈɒf/
leave the ground and rise into the air (a plane, a helicopter, a bird)
The rescue helicopter could not take off until the wind dropped.
a blog /blɒɡ/
a website where one person regularly writes about their ideas or experiences
Lan writes a blog about cadet life, with photos from every field trip and a list of the best cheap noodle stalls.
a scientist /ˈsaɪəntɪst/
a person whose job is to study how the natural world works
The scientists at the weather centre use satellite images to follow a storm hour by hour.
Possible or not
unlikely /ʌnˈlaɪkli/
probably not going to happen or be true
It's unlikely that the bus will leave on time in this rain, so let's wait inside.
impossible /ɪmˈpɒsəbl/
not able to happen or to be true in any way
Without a boat, it was impossible to reach the patients on the other side of the flooded river.
imagine /ɪˈmædʒɪn/
make a picture of something in your mind

10 functions · 30 chunks

1 · Describing extreme weather

  • It's absolutely pouring / freezing out there.
  • We had the worst … I've ever seen.
  • The wind was so strong that …

The wind was so strong that it bent the flagpole outside the lecture hall.

2 · Warning about danger and staying safe

  • Keep away from … until …
  • Whatever you do, don't …
  • It's much safer to … than to …

Keep away from the riverbank until the water level drops.

3 · Imagining an unlikely situation

  • If I …, I'd …
  • Just imagine if …
  • If I were in that situation, I'd probably …

If I were in that situation, I'd probably call the duty officer before doing anything else.

4 · Asking what someone would do

  • What would you do if …?
  • Would you ever … if …?
  • How would you feel if …?

How would you feel if you had to spend a month at a remote island clinic?

5 · Talking about hopes and dreams

  • One day I'd love to …
  • I'm hoping to … after I graduate.
  • If I could choose any job, I'd …

One day I'd love to join a medical team that flies out to disaster zones.

6 · Describing a natural place

  • It's a … place, full of …
  • What I like most about it is …
  • It's surrounded by …

It's surrounded by limestone hills, and early in the morning the river is completely still.

7 · Saying nature is everywhere (or nowhere)

  • There's something living in almost every …
  • You can find nature almost anywhere, even …
  • There was nothing but … / nowhere to …

There's something living in almost every handful of soil, if you look closely enough.

8 · Asking questions with any-

  • Is there anywhere … near here?
  • Did anyone … while I was out?
  • Have you seen anything … lately?

Did anyone call from the hospital while I was out?

9 · Explaining a cause

  • This happens because …
  • … is caused by …
  • One of the main reasons for … is …

Many sports injuries are caused by skipping the warm-up.

10 · Explaining an effect or a consequence

  • As a result, …
  • This means that …
  • … leads to …

Too little sleep before an exam leads to slow thinking and careless mistakes.

From B1 to B1+ / B2: 12 upgrade pairs

B1B1+ / B2
It rained a lot and the river came into the town.Three days of heavy rain pushed the river over its banks, and by morning it had flooded the lower streets.
The storm broke a lot of things.The storm caused serious damage: roofs were torn off, power lines came down and two bridges were closed.
The radio said a typhoon is coming, so people left their houses.After the warning on the radio, the authorities evacuated every family living near the shore.
Storm chasers do very dangerous things.Storm chasers drive straight towards tornadoes that everyone else is running away from.
If I win a lot of money, I will stop studying.If I won a lot of money, I'd still finish my degree; I've worked far too hard to stop now.
I want to work in another country.My dream is to spend a few years as a doctor overseas and then bring what I learn back home.
You should take a coat.If I were you, I'd take a coat; it gets freezing on the pass after dark.
There are many trees near my house.There's a nearby green space with old trees, a small pond and a path that stays quiet after dark.

There is not any place to sit.The waiting room was so crowded that there was nowhere left to sit, so the cadets stood by the door.

No rain is bad for farmers.A long drought means smaller harvests, higher food prices and, in the end, more hungry families.

The answer frame — 7 steps

Sample question: ‘If you could protect one natural place in Vietnam, which would you choose and why?’

1Point

Answer at once: name your place.

If I could protect just one place, I'd choose …

2Why

Give the main reason it deserves protection.

The main reason is that …

3How

Show what that reason means on the ground.

What makes it worth saving is …

4Example

Tell one specific case: a visit, a fact, a person.

When I went there, …

5Result

Say what that one case led to.

Because of that, …

6Limitation

Admit a weak point or the other side.

Admittedly, …

7Evaluation

Weigh it up and look ahead; don't repeat the Point.

Still, … / In the long run, …

Model answer · all seven steps in a single paragraph

In the model answers: Point = step of the answer frame · frame language = opinion, reason, example, contrast, conclusion · unit vocabulary = a word or phrase from the four Sheet 3 groups

PointIf I could protect just one place in Vietnam, I'd choose the Cần Giờ mangrove forest, where Hồ Chí Minh City meets the sea. WhyThe main reason is that it protects people as well as wildlife: the trees stand between the city and the sea. HowTheir roots hold the mud together and slow the waves down, so when a storm pushes the sea inland, the water has lost a lot of its power by the time it reaches the villages behind them. ExampleWhen I went there with my family a few years ago, a ranger told us that chemicals sprayed during the war had destroyed most of the forest, and that people started replanting it by hand in 1978. ResultBecause of all that planting, Cần Giờ became Vietnam's first UNESCO biosphere reserve in 2000, and the wildlife came back. That afternoon we watched monkeys and huge flocks of birds in trees that are younger than my dad. LimitationAdmittedly, it doesn't look as impressive in photos as Hạ Long Bay, and the heat, the mud and the mosquitoes keep a lot of tourists away. EvaluationStill, a forest that grew back after the war had wiped out most of it shows that damage can be undone, and if typhoons keep getting stronger, that wall of trees could matter even more to the city in twenty years than it does now.

Where to use it
  • Speaking Part 1: only Point → Why → Example, in about thirty seconds.
  • Speaking Part 2: spread the seven steps over the cue-card prompts and save the Evaluation for the last line, the one that starts ‘and explain …’.
  • Speaking Part 3: all seven steps in about a minute, one short sentence for each.
  • Cause–effect paragraph (Sheet 8): the paragraph has its own frame, but each cause or effect borrows Why → How → Example → Result, and the last sentence sums up like an Evaluation, with nothing new in it.

12 common mistakes

MistakeCorrectionRemember
If the bus would come on time, we'd never be late for roll call.If the bus came on time, we'd never be late for roll call.never would in the if clause: use the past simple.
If the road were open we'd drive straight to the camp.If the road were open, we'd drive straight to the camp.if clause first → comma · main clause first → no comma.
If the bus is late again, we would take a taxi.If the bus is late again, we'll take a taxi.a real chance → if + present, will; keep would for imagined situations.
If I was you, I'd see a doctor about that cough.If I were you, I'd see a doctor about that cough.advice uses the fixed phrase If I were you.
We didn't find nothing in the old bunker.We didn't find anything in the old bunker.not + any-, or no- alone: never both (MLH p. 43).
Anybody came to the lecture because of the storm.Nobody came to the lecture because of the storm.any- is not negative on its own: use no-, or not + any-.
Everybody in the ward are asleep.Everybody in the ward is asleep.every-, some-, any-, no- words take a singular verb (MLH p. 13).
Nothing didn't move in the forest all night.Nothing moved in the forest all night.nothing, nobody, no one as the subject → a positive verb.
Did you see interesting anything at the museum?Did you see anything interesting at the museum?the adjective comes after the pronoun (MLH p. 59).
We should protect the nature for our children.We should protect nature for our children.nature = the natural world: no the.
The tall pine next to our camp was hit by a lightening.The tall pine next to our camp was hit by lightning.lightning: no e, no a (lightening = making lighter) · a flash of lightning.
The typhoon had a huge affect on the town because of the dykes were too low.The typhoon had a huge effect on the town because the dykes were too low.effect (noun) on · affect (verb) · because + clause · because of + noun.

What if …?

Randall Monroe is a scientist and he used to work for NASA. One day he started a blog called What if …? Every week people send Randall questions about unlikely or impossible things, and Randall gives scientific answers.

Here are some What … if …? questions about weather and nature.

What would happen if lightning hit you in a submarine? What if you were in a boat?

If you were in a submarine, you'd be safe because you'd be underwater. However, lightning usually hits the tallest thing, so if you were on a flat surface, like in a boat on the sea, you wouldn't be as safe.

Would I be safe if I was in a swimming pool during a thunderstorm?

You wouldn't be safe if your head was above the water. Lightning might hit you. And if the lightning hit the water near you, the electrical energy would spread outwards across the water.

If it was raining, how fast would you have to drive to break the car windscreen?

The rain would break the glass if you drove at the speed of sound. But if you did that, the car would take off! Rain wouldn't break the glass if you drove at a normal speed. But in freezing temperatures, hail would break the windscreen if you drove fast. In fact, that sometimes happens in some parts of the world.

1What is the main purpose of Randall's blog?
1What is the main purpose of Randall's blog?
Readers send questions about ‘unlikely or impossible things’ and Randall ‘gives scientific answers’: the situations are imagined, but the science is real. NASA is only where he used to work, and nobody sends in real disasters or stories they have lived through.Clue: First paragraph: unlikely or impossible things + scientific answers.
In the text: One day he started a blog called What if …? Every week people send Randall questions about unlikely or impossible things, and Randall gives scientific answers.
2Randall Monroe is a scientist and he used to work for NASA. What can we infer?
2Randall Monroe is a scientist and he used to work for NASA. What can we infer?
NASA belongs to his past (SB Ex 4.1: No). The present tense in is a scientist shows he is still a scientist, and the text never connects NASA with the blog.Clue: used to + verb = a past habit or state that is not true now.
In the text: Randall Monroe is a scientist and he used to work for NASA.
3Which of these questions would Randall most probably answer on his blog?
3Which of these questions would Randall most probably answer on his blog?
A whole year of rain without a break is not going to happen, but science can still say what it would do, so it fits. The other questions ask for a forecast, a date, a shopping tip or a number: practical facts with no imagined situation in them.Clue: The blog takes questions about unlikely or impossible things.
In the text: Every week people send Randall questions about unlikely or impossible things, and Randall gives scientific answers.
4According to the first answer, why would you be in more danger in a small boat than in a submarine?
4According to the first answer, why would you be in more danger in a small boat than in a submarine?
On open water nothing stands higher than a boat, so the boat becomes the tallest thing around. The submarine is safe for a different reason: it is underwater. The text says nothing about metal, special equipment, waves or speed.Clue: However, lightning usually hits the tallest thing, so …
In the text: However, lightning usually hits the tallest thing, so if you were on a flat surface, like in a boat on the sea, you wouldn't be as safe.
5… like in a boat on the sea, you wouldn't be as safe. As safe as what?
5… like in a boat on the sea, you wouldn't be as safe. As safe as what?
The first sentence says ‘If you were in a submarine, you'd be safe’, and the boat is compared with that: less safe than the submarine. The swimming pool and the car only come in later answers, and the tallest thing is where lightning goes, not a safe place.Clue: as safe compares with something in the sentence before.
In the text: If you were in a submarine, you'd be safe because you'd be underwater. However, lightning usually hits the tallest thing, so if you were on a flat surface, like in a boat on the sea, you wouldn't be as safe.
6Lightning might hit you. Which sentence means almost the same?
6Lightning might hit you. Which sentence means almost the same?
Randall cannot promise that you would be hit, only that it could happen, and that is enough to make you unsafe. Would certainly or has to would turn it into a certainty, and might here is about now or the future, not the past.Clue: might + verb = a possibility, weaker than would (the second conditional often uses could or might in the result).
In the text: Lightning might hit you.
7… the electrical energy would spread outwards across the water. What does spread outwards mean?
7… the electrical energy would spread outwards across the water. What does spread outwards mean?
The lightning hits the water at one point near you, and from there its energy travels across the surface in every direction, like rings on a pond. That is how it can reach a swimmer it did not hit.Clue: TB note: spread outwards = move away from a central point in all directions.
In the text: And if the lightning hit the water near you, the electrical energy would spread outwards across the water.
8What does the answer about the swimming pool suggest?
8What does the answer about the swimming pool suggest?
The first danger is a direct hit on your head. The second is different: lightning hits the water near you and the energy spreads across it, so it reaches you anyway. The text never says water protects a swimmer, and it does not compare indoor and outdoor pools.Clue: Two dangers: Lightning might hit you and if the lightning hit the water near you …
In the text: You wouldn't be safe if your head was above the water. Lightning might hit you. And if the lightning hit the water near you, the electrical energy would spread outwards across the water.
9But if you did that, the car would take off! What does the writer mean?
9But if you did that, the car would take off! What does the writer mean?
did that points back to driving ‘at the speed of sound’, about 1,200 km/h (TB). At that speed a car would rise off the road, so nobody could ever really test the idea. Take off here has nothing to do with removing something.Clue: take off = leave the ground and start to fly, like a plane.
In the text: The rain would break the glass if you drove at the speed of sound. But if you did that, the car would take off!
10Why does the writer end the car would take off with an exclamation mark?
10Why does the writer end the car would take off with an exclamation mark?
A flying car is a surprising, slightly silly result, and the ! shares the joke with the reader. Straight afterwards he goes back to the science (a normal speed, then hail), so he is having fun, not complaining, warning or admitting a mistake.Clue: Tone: an exclamation mark after an amazing or funny idea.
In the text: But if you did that, the car would take off!
11In fact, that sometimes happens in some parts of the world. What does that refer to?
11In fact, that sometimes happens in some parts of the world. What does that refer to?
‘But in freezing temperatures, hail would break the windscreen if you drove fast.’ That is the only situation in the answer that really happens; rain at a normal speed would not break the glass, and nobody drives at the speed of sound.Clue: Reference: that points back to the sentence just before it.
In the text: Rain wouldn't break the glass if you drove at a normal speed. But in freezing temperatures, hail would break the windscreen if you drove fast. In fact, that sometimes happens in some parts of the world.
12What do the three answers have in common?
12What do the three answers have in common?
All three start from an imagined situation (If you were …, You wouldn't be safe if …, The rain would break the glass if …) and then explain it: you'd be underwater, the energy would spread, only hail and a fast car would break the glass. The third is about rain and hail, not lightning, and two of the answers say you would not be safe.Clue: Global: look at how each answer starts and at the reason it gives.
In the text: If you were in a submarine, you'd be safe because you'd be underwater. You wouldn't be safe if your head was above the water. The rain would break the glass if you drove at the speed of sound. But in freezing temperatures, hail would break the windscreen if you drove fast.

Extra practice · PET Reading Part 3 · Roy Sullivan: the man lightning hit seven times

Questions 11–15. Read the article about an American park ranger and answer the five questions. Choose the right answer each time.

Passage | Questions

Roy Sullivan: the man lightning hit seven times

Most people will never be hit by lightning, not even once. Roy Sullivan, a park ranger in the US state of Virginia, was hit seven times between 1942 and 1977, and he survived every strike. Guinness World Records still lists him as the person struck by lightning the most recorded times.Q11

Sullivan began working in Shenandoah National Park in 1936. The first strike came in April 1942. He was sheltering from a storm in a new fire lookout tower, a tall building for watching over the forest, but the tower had no lightning rod. When lightning started hitting it, he ran out, and he was struck a few steps from the door.Q12 It burned a line down his right leg and left a hole in his shoe.

Then nothing happened for twenty-seven years. In July 1969, lightning hit the trees beside a mountain road and came in through the open window of his truck. It knocked him unconscious and burned off his eyebrows and eyelashes. A year later, it hit a power transformer near his house and jumped to his left shoulder.

After his hair caught fire inside a ranger station in 1972, Sullivan began to fear that the next strike would kill him. From then on, he carried water in his truck, and whenever a storm came, he pulled over and lay down until it had passed.Q13 It did not help much. He was hit again in 1973 while he was out on patrol, in 1976, and for the last time in 1977, while he was fishing.Q13

Being famous for lightning was lonely. Other people did not want to stand next to him when the sky went dark. Once, when there was lightning far away, a chief ranger walked off with the words ‘I'll see you later.’Q14 Sullivan found this very sad. The head of the park recorded all seven, but he never saw any of them himself, and much of the story rests on Sullivan's own word, so some people doubt parts of it.Q15

11What does the first paragraph tell us about Roy Sullivan?
11What does the first paragraph tell us about Roy Sullivan?
He was struck ‘seven times’, and Guinness lists him as ‘the person struck by lightning the most recorded times’, so no one has more recorded strikes. The strikes were spread over thirty-five years, and the article never calls him the first person to survive one.Clue: Paragraph 1: Guinness World Records still lists him as …
In the text: Most people will never be hit by lightning, not even once. Roy Sullivan, a park ranger in the US state of Virginia, was hit seven times between 1942 and 1977, and he survived every strike. Guinness World Records still lists him as the person struck by lightning the most recorded times.
12What happened in April 1942?
12What happened in April 1942?
The tower had nothing to protect it, so he left it, and the lightning hit him just outside. He was not watching from the top, nothing says the tower caught fire, and the hole in his shoe was damage, not a lost shoe.Clue: Paragraph 2: the tower had no lightning rod … he ran out, and he was struck a few steps from the door.
In the text: The first strike came in April 1942. He was sheltering from a storm in a new fire lookout tower, a tall building for watching over the forest, but the tower had no lightning rod. When lightning started hitting it, he ran out, and he was struck a few steps from the door.
13How did Sullivan change after 1972?
13How did Sullivan change after 1972?
After 1972 he carried water and pulled over to lie down whenever a storm came: ways of protecting himself. He kept working in the park (he was hit on patrol in 1973), so he did not stop working outdoors or move away.Clue: Paragraph 4: began to fear … From then on, he …
In the text: After his hair caught fire inside a ranger station in 1972, Sullivan began to fear that the next strike would kill him. From then on, he carried water in his truck, and whenever a storm came, he pulled over and lay down until it had passed. He was hit again in 1973 while he was out on patrol, in 1976, and for the last time in 1977, while he was fishing.
14Why does the writer tell the story of the chief ranger?
14Why does the writer tell the story of the chief ranger?
The chief ranger is one example of this: when lightning was far away, he walked off with ‘I'll see you later.’ The point is that people were afraid to stand near Sullivan, not that they disliked or disbelieved him, and nobody else was hit.Clue: Paragraph 5: Other people did not want to stand next to him …
In the text: Being famous for lightning was lonely. Other people did not want to stand next to him when the sky went dark. Once, when there was lightning far away, a chief ranger walked off with the words “I'll see you later.”
15Which of these best describes the writer's view of Sullivan's story?
15Which of these best describes the writer's view of Sullivan's story?
The writer clearly finds the record amazing, but says honestly that the head of the park ‘never saw any of them himself’ and that ‘much of the story rests on Sullivan's own word, so some people doubt parts of it.’ That is neither ‘completely invented’ (the strikes were recorded) nor ‘proved by people who saw the strikes’.Clue: Global: the last paragraph + the facts the writer chooses.
In the text: The head of the park recorded all seven, but he never saw any of them himself, and much of the story rests on Sullivan's own word, so some people doubt parts of it.

Extra practice · PET Reading Part 4 · The night the river came into town

Questions 16–20. A cadet tells the story of a flood-relief mission. Five sentences are missing from the story: for each gap, choose the sentence (A–F) under the text that fits it. You will not need one sentence.

Passage | Questions

The night the river came into town

Last October, after three days of heavy rain, our team of medical cadets was sent to a small town in central Vietnam that the floodwater had cut off from the rest of the province. I had seen floods on the news many times, but never with my own eyes.Q16 (16) …………… The road ended at a primary school on a hill, which had become home for about two hundred people.Q16

Our job sounded simple: check everyone, treat small injuries and stop anyone getting ill from the dirty water.Q17 (17) …………… Most of our patients had cuts on their feet from walking through the water, and hardly anyone had slept.Q17

On the second night, just after midnight, a fisherman arrived at the school in a small boat, soaking wet and out of breath.Q18 (18) …………… Captain Nam chose two of us to go back with him, and I was one of them.Q18

The boat moved slowly along streets that had turned into a river.Q16 We found Mrs Tư on the roof of her kitchen, holding a torch in one hand and a bag of rice in the other.Q19 (19) …………… We all laughed, and she laughed too, and we promised to go back for them in the morning.Q19

We never found the chickens.Q19,Q20 (20) …………… I have treated many patients since then, but whenever I hear heavy rain at night, I think of her standing by that road.Q20

A In practice, it meant forty patients before lunch and a queue that never seemed to get any shorter.

B She was cold and frightened, but the first thing she asked about was her chickens.

C From the back of the army truck, I watched brown water cover the rice fields as far as I could see.

D By the next morning, the water had gone down and the town was dry again.

E His neighbour, an old woman who lived alone, had refused to leave her house, and the water was still rising.

F But when we left the town a week later, Mrs Tư was waiting by the road with a bag of bananas for the whole team.

16Gap 16
16Gap 16
C: the writer now sees a flood for the first time, ‘From the back of the army truck’, and the truck's road then ends at the school. D (the water had gone) fits nowhere: on the second night the streets are still a river.Clue: Before the gap: never with my own eyes; after it: The road ended at …
In the text: I had seen floods on the news many times, but never with my own eyes. The road ended at a primary school on a hill, which had become home for about two hundred people. The boat moved slowly along streets that had turned into a river.
17Gap 17
17Gap 17
A: ‘In practice, it meant forty patients before lunch …’ sounded simple → In practice contrasts the plan with reality, and the next sentence describes those patients.Clue: Before the gap: Our job sounded simple. Which sentence shows what it was really like?
In the text: Our job sounded simple: check everyone, treat small injuries and stop anyone getting ill from the dirty water. Most of our patients had cuts on their feet from walking through the water, and hardly anyone had slept.
18Gap 18
18Gap 18
E tells us why he came: his neighbour ‘had refused to leave her house, and the water was still rising.’ That is the reason for the rescue trip in the next sentence.Clue: Before: a fisherman arrives by boat at midnight; after: Captain Nam sends two cadets back with him.
In the text: On the second night, just after midnight, a fisherman arrived at the school in a small boat, soaking wet and out of breath. Captain Nam chose two of us to go back with him, and I was one of them.
19Gap 19
19Gap 19
B: ‘the first thing she asked about was her chickens.’ That is what makes everyone laugh, and them = the chickens, which the next paragraph says they never found.Clue: After the gap: We all laughed … go back for them. Who or what are them?

20Gap 20
F: ‘But when we left the town a week later, Mrs Tư was waiting by the road with a bag of bananas …’ But contrasts with the lost chickens, and that road points back to it.Clue: Before: We never found the chickens. After: I think of her standing by that road.

After reading · Talk about it

Answer each question in one paragraph that goes through all seven steps: Point → Why → How → Example → Result → Limitation → Evaluation.

1 · Why do people enjoy asking “What if …?” questions about impossible things?

Model answer

PointI think it's because an impossible question lets you play with huge ideas without any real risk. WhyBecause nothing is at stake, people dare to follow an idea much further than they would in class. HowYou pick one rule of nature, break it, and then follow the science step by step to see where it leads. ExampleLast term someone in my platoon wondered aloud whether a mosquito the size of a dog could survive, and six of us spent a whole evening arguing about it over a whiteboard. ResultBy the end of the evening we'd worked out that a giant mosquito probably couldn't even breathe properly, because insects take in air through tiny holes along their bodies, and the next day two of us borrowed a book on insect anatomy from the library. LimitationAdmittedly, some people see these questions as a waste of time when there are real problems to solve. EvaluationOn balance, they're one of the cheapest ways to make people curious about how the world really works.

2 · Should science be taught through strange questions like the ones on Randall's blog?

Model answer

PointYes, but as a way into a lesson, not as the whole lesson. WhyA strange question makes students want the answer before they've even seen a formula. HowThe teacher opens with the puzzle, lets everyone guess, and only then brings in the science that settles it. ExampleIn our first-year physics module, the lecturer opened the electricity topic with a single puzzle: would we be safe in a car if lightning struck it? ResultMost of us said yes because of the rubber tyres: the right answer for the wrong reason. It's the car's metal body that carries the current round the people inside, and nobody in that room has forgotten it since. LimitationOf course, there isn't time to turn every topic into a puzzle, and exams still test the dull basics. EvaluationEven so, two or three good puzzles a term would make the dry parts much easier to sit through.

3 · What is the safest thing to do if a thunderstorm starts while you are outdoors on a field exercise?

Model answer

PointStop the exercise and get everyone into a proper building or a hard-topped vehicle, fast. WhyNo place outside is safe once you can hear thunder, because lightning can strike up to about sixteen kilometres from the storm. HowIn practice, the officer calls it off, the unit leaves the open ground and the tall trees, and everyone waits in a bus or a closed cab, never under a canvas cover, until thirty minutes after the last rumble. ExampleOn a map-reading exercise last May, our instructor heard thunder at about three o'clock and ordered all forty of us onto the bus, even though it wasn't raining yet. ResultTwenty minutes later lightning hit the hill we'd just left, and suddenly nobody minded losing the afternoon. LimitationIf there's no shelter at all, you can only lower the risk: keep away from tall trees and water, and spread the group out so that if one person is hit, the others can give first aid. EvaluationTraining in the rain is part of the job, but training in a thunderstorm is a risk that no exercise is worth.

4 · Should scientists spend time answering the public's questions online?

Model answer

PointI think they should, as long as it doesn't eat into their research. WhyMost people never meet a real scientist, so an online answer may be the only time they hear science explained by someone who actually does it. HowEven an hour a week of short replies or videos can reach thousands of people who don't read science journals. ExampleRandall's blog is a good case: in 2014 it grew into a book, What If? ResultIt went straight to number one on the New York Times bestseller list, so people who'd never pick up a physics textbook were suddenly reading about physics for fun. LimitationThen again, the internet is full of angry comments and false claims, and answering them can swallow hours that a scientist simply hasn't got. EvaluationThe best balance, I'd say, is a few careful answers chosen well rather than trying to reply to everyone.

Before you listen: imagine that summers in your home town became five degrees hotter, every year. Would you stay, or would you move? Where to?

Listen (SB p. 143 Ex 9) to two friends, Speakers A and B, two or three times, and answer Questions 1–6 about what they mean and how they feel.

Transcript

AWould you move to another country if the weather became much hotter in your country?Q1,Q6

BWould you?Q3

1What are the two speakers talking about?
1What are the two speakers talking about?
A asks a What would you do if …? kind of question, and both answer it. Nobody is planning a trip, reporting a forecast or explaining climate change; the pool is only part of B's answer.Clue: The first line sets the topic: Would you move to another country if …?
In the text: Would you move to another country if the weather became much hotter in your country?
2How does Speaker B feel about the idea of much hotter weather?
2How does Speaker B feel about the idea of much hotter weather?
B says no to moving because ‘I'd love it if the weather became hotter’, and at the end pictures spending ‘every day outside by the pool’. That is a clear, happy opinion, with no worry or doubt in it.Clue: No, I'd love it if …
In the text: No, I'd love it if the weather became hotter. I'd spend every day outside by the pool.
3Would you? Why does Speaker B ask this short question?
3Would you? Why does Speaker B ask this short question?
A has just said ‘I'd go and live somewhere else’, the opposite of B's view, so B reacts with surprise. A hears it as a request to confirm and answers ‘Yes, I wouldn't want to stay.’ B is not agreeing, inviting or asking for a place.Clue: A short question such as Would you? or Do you? reacts to what the other person has just said.
In the text: I'd go and live somewhere else. Would you? Yes, I wouldn't want to stay.
4Which line shows that Speaker A has a clear idea of the kind of place to move to?
4Which line shows that Speaker A has a clear idea of the kind of place to move to?
‘Somewhere else’ only means ‘not here’. A's last line is more exact: the new country must be colder. The pool line is B's, and it is about staying, not moving.Clue: somewhere else is vague; a country with a colder climate names the kind of place.
In the text: I'd go and live somewhere else. I'd find a country with a colder climate.
5Oh, I wouldn't. What wouldn't Speaker B do?
5Oh, I wouldn't. What wouldn't Speaker B do?
A says ‘I'd find a country with a colder climate’; B answers ‘Oh, I wouldn't [find one]’ and then says what B would do instead: stay and enjoy the pool. So B would stay, enjoy the heat and go outside.Clue: Ellipsis: I wouldn't = I wouldn't + the verb the other speaker has just used.
In the text: I'd find a country with a colder climate. Oh, I wouldn't. I'd spend every day outside by the pool.
6Why do both speakers use would and past forms like became?
6Why do both speakers use would and past forms like became?
became looks like the past, but here it means ‘if it happened, now or later’. Neither speaker says the weather has changed or that they have plans; they are only imagining how they would react.Clue: if + past simple, would + verb = an imagined or unlikely situation (Sheet 4 · the second conditional).
In the text: Would you move to another country if the weather became much hotter in your country? No, I'd love it if the weather became hotter.

Listening B · Track 96 · Nature in one cubic foot

Before you listen (SB p. 144 Ex 2–3): which of these places do you see every day: a forest, a mountain, a field, a river, a garden, an ocean, a park, a desert? Where near the academy could you find wild plants and animals?

Listen (SB Ex 4–5) to part of a documentary about the photographer David Liittschwager and answer Questions 1–8: why the documentary starts as it does, what he wanted to show, how he worked and what the speaker means.

Audio + transcript | Questions
Played 0×

The transcript opens when you press Show answers.

Transcript

If you live in the middle of the city, maybe you think that there's nowhere to look at nature.Q1 Or if you have a local park, perhaps you don't see anything except people walking their dogs.Q2 However, David Liittschwager, the photographer, wants to show us that everyone can find nature. Different species of plants and animals are always somewhere nearby.Q1,Q3

David spent five years recording living things in different places around the world.Q5 He used a green metal frame which measured one cubic foot and took it to different locations.Q4 Then he spent three weeks in that place and photographed everything living inside the green metal cube.Q4,Q5,Q6 That included leaves, animals, plants, fish, even living things which were smaller than one millimetre in size.Q6,Q7 Some of his photos were taken in places far away from any towns, such as the middle of a forest, the side of a mountain, the ocean or a river, but some of them were taken in parks in the middle of cities.Q8

cube (n) /kjuːb/ a shape like a box that has six equal square sides (cubic = adj)

1Why does the documentary begin with If you live in the middle of the city …?
1Why does the documentary begin with If you live in the middle of the city …?
The speaker starts with what many city people believe (‘there's nowhere to look at nature’) and then turns it round with However: ‘everyone can find nature’. The opening is the mistaken idea that the rest of the documentary corrects.Clue: maybe you think … and then However, …
In the text: If you live in the middle of the city, maybe you think that there's nowhere to look at nature. However, David Liittschwager, the photographer, wants to show us that everyone can find nature. Different species of plants and animals are always somewhere nearby.
2… perhaps you don't see anything except people walking their dogs. What point is the speaker making?
2… perhaps you don't see anything except people walking their dogs. What point is the speaker making?
The dog walkers are simply the most obvious thing in a park. The speaker means that plants, insects and other living things are there too, but people don't notice them; nothing is said against dogs or their owners.Clue: you don't see anything except … = the only thing you notice is …
In the text: Or if you have a local park, perhaps you don't see anything except people walking their dogs.
3What does David Liittschwager want people to understand?
3What does David Liittschwager want people to understand?
‘everyone can find nature. Different species of plants and animals are always somewhere nearby.’ Everyone and always somewhere nearby include city people too. Nothing in the recording is about new species, protection or moving house.Clue: wants to show us that …
In the text: However, David Liittschwager, the photographer, wants to show us that everyone can find nature. Different species of plants and animals are always somewhere nearby.
4What was the green metal frame for?
4What was the green metal frame for?
The frame was always the same size (one cubic foot: a cube about 30 cm on each side) and went to every location, so each time it marked out one small space. Then he photographed what lived inside it; nothing says it held a camera or trapped animals.Clue: a green metal frame which measured one cubic foot … photographed everything living inside the green metal cube
In the text: He used a green metal frame which measured one cubic foot and took it to different locations. Then he spent three weeks in that place and photographed everything living inside the green metal cube.
5How long did the whole project take, and how long did he stay in each place?
5How long did the whole project take, and how long did he stay in each place?
‘David spent five years recording living things …’ is the whole project; ‘Then he spent three weeks in that place’ is each location (that is why SB Ex 5.4 is false).Clue: Two lengths of time: spent five years … and spent three weeks in that place.
In the text: David spent five years recording living things in different places around the world. Then he spent three weeks in that place and photographed everything living inside the green metal cube.
6What did he photograph inside the cube?
6What did he photograph inside the cube?
Everything living means he did not choose: ‘leaves, animals, plants, fish, even living things which were smaller than one millimetre in size’. So the tiniest creatures were in the photos too (SB Ex 5.5: false), and fish were only one group.Clue: photographed everything living … + That included …
In the text: Then he spent three weeks in that place and photographed everything living inside the green metal cube. That included leaves, animals, plants, fish, even living things which were smaller than one millimetre in size.
7… even living things which were smaller than one millimetre in size. Why does the speaker use even?
7… even living things which were smaller than one millimetre in size. Why does the speaker use even?
Leaves, plants and fish are what you expect; a creature smaller than a millimetre (0.1 cm, TB) is not. Even shows how complete his work was: he left nothing out.Clue: even adds the most surprising item to a list.
In the text: That included leaves, animals, plants, fish, even living things which were smaller than one millimetre in size.
8What does the last sentence tell us about the places?
8What does the last sentence tell us about the places?
The forest, the mountain, the ocean and the river are ‘far away from any towns’, ‘but some of them were taken in parks in the middle of cities’. That brings the documentary back to its first point: nature is near city people too.Clue: Some … such as …, but some of them …
In the text: Some of his photos were taken in places far away from any towns, such as the middle of a forest, the side of a mountain, the ocean or a river, but some of them were taken in parks in the middle of cities.

Transcript

Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Cúc Phương. My name's Hiền, and I'll be your guide today. We're about a hundred and twenty kilometres south of Hà Nội, so thank you for getting up so early! Many visitors think the park is quite new, but in fact it became Vietnam's very first national park in nineteen sixty-two.Q14 It's huge, too: more than twenty-two thousand hectares of forest and limestone hills.

Our first stop is the Endangered Primate Rescue Centre, which opened in nineteen ninety-three. It looks after langurs, gibbons and lorises. The lorises are the small ones with very big eyes.Q15 They're active at night, so they'll probably be asleep when we get there. Close by is the Turtle Conservation Centre, which opened in nineteen ninety-eight, where you can see some of Vietnam's rarest turtles.Q14,Q15

If you'd like to come back in the spring, try to visit between late April and the end of May. That's butterfly season, when there are butterflies everywhere you look.Q16 Today you'll see more birds than butterflies: there are around three hundred kinds of bird in the park.

After lunch, we'll walk up to the Cave of Prehistoric Man. In the nineteen sixties, archaeologists found three graves there that are about seven thousand five hundred years old. People sometimes hear ‘seventy-five thousand’, but it's seven and a half thousand.Q17 Stone tools were found in the cave too.

Now, a few practical things. Lunch is at half past twelve at the visitor centre.Q19 If you get lost on a forest path, don't panic: the park office's phone number is on the back of your ticket, not on the map.Q18 And your tickets say the bus back to Hà Nội leaves at half past four, but we've changed that to four o'clock, so please be back by then.Q19 Right, let's go and meet the primates.

Transcript

PresenterGood evening, and welcome to Nature Near You. My guest tonight is Dr Linh Pham, a junior doctor at a big city hospital, whose photographs of insects and plants in the hospital garden are now in an exhibition at the city library. Linh, how did it all start?

LinhCompletely by accident. I was on night shifts in my first year, and during my break I used to go out into the garden for some fresh air. One night I noticed a moth on the wall with two big spots on its wings that looked exactly like eyes. I took a photo with my phoneQ20, and the next morning I couldn't stop looking at it.

PresenterAnd you kept going back?

LinhEvery break. What amazed me was how much was living in such an ordinary place. It's just a small garden between two car parks, but in one flower bed I counted more than forty kinds of insect in a single month.Q21 Before that, I'd walked past it every day without seeing anything.

PresenterDo you need expensive equipment for this kind of photography?

LinhPeople always assume I've got a big camera, but I use my phone and a little clip-on lens that cost me less than a hundred thousand dong. The real secret is patience.Q22 Insects don't wait for you.

PresenterWhat do your patients think?

LinhThat's the best part. I started putting a photo of the week on the noticeboard in our ward. Now some of the long-stay patients go out in their wheelchairs looking for things, and they come back and tell me where they've seen a beetle or a strange flower. One man found a stick insect I'd been looking for for weeks.Q23

PresenterHas anything gone wrong?

LinhOh, yes. Last summer the gardeners cut down a whole corner of tall grass where I'd been photographing a family of spiders. I was upset at first, but I went and talked to them, and now they leave one small corner of the garden wild.Q24 They even call me when they find something interesting.

PresenterOne last question: what would you tell someone who wants to give it a go?

LinhDon't wait for a holiday in a national park. Choose one small space near you, a window box or a tree outside your door, and look at it closely for ten minutes.Q25 You'll be surprised by what's there.

PresenterDr Linh Pham, thank you.

Sheet 7 / 11 · Speaking · Part 1 interview · Part 2 long turn (cards A and B) · Part 3 discussion

Speaking

In the model answers: Point = step of the answer frame · frame language = opinion, reason, example, contrast, conclusion · unit vocabulary = words and chunks from Groups 1–4

Part 1 · Interview — 10 short questions on 3 topics, about 30 seconds per answer

0:30Answer = Point → Why → Example
Record practice — Part 1

Let's talk about weather and seasons.

1 · Which season do you like best where you live?

  • PointDefinitely …, when the … stops for a while.
  • WhyThe air finally feels … after …, and the whole city …
  • ExampleOne morning last …, for example, we did our … in the cool air, and for once nobody …
Model answer

PointDefinitely autumn, when the heavy rain stops for a while. WhyThe air finally feels dry after the sticky summer, and the whole city smells of milk flowers. ExampleOne morning last October, for example, we did our six o'clock run round the parade ground in the cool air, and for once nobody in my platoon complained.

2 · How often do you check the weather forecast?

  • PointEvery …, usually just before …
  • WhyWe have a lot of … training, so I need to know whether I'll be …
  • ExampleLast week, for instance, the app showed … for …, so I packed …, and I was the only one in … who …
Model answer

PointEvery single night, usually just before lights out. WhyWe have a lot of outdoor training, so I need to know whether I'll be soaked, freezing or fine. ExampleLast week, for instance, the app showed a thunderstorm for Thursday afternoon, so I packed a raincoat for shooting practice, and I was the only one in my platoon who came back dry.

3 · Have you ever been caught outside in a really bad storm?

  • PointYes, once, and I still remember …
  • WhySummer storms in the north can go from … to … in about …, so …
  • ExampleTwo summers ago, for example, I was … when …, and I spent an hour under … with …
Model answer

PointYes, once, and I still remember how fast it happened. WhySummer storms in the north can go from sunshine to thunder in about ten minutes, so you don't get much warning. ExampleTwo summers ago, for example, I was cycling home from my uncle's farm when the sky went black, and I spent an hour under a petrol station roof with half the village.

4 · If you could change anything about the weather in your home town, what would you change?

  • PointI'd get rid of …
  • WhyFor weeks …, and if the air were …, I'd …
  • ExampleLast March, for example, my … took … to dry on …, and I had to … before …
Model answer

PointI'd get rid of the damp spell we get at the end of winter. WhyFor weeks the walls and floors are wet, and if the air were drier, I'd stop feeling sticky all day. ExampleLast March, for example, my uniform took four days to dry on the balcony, and I had to iron it still damp before a morning inspection.

Let's talk about nature and places near you.

5 · Is there anywhere near your academy where you can enjoy a bit of nature?

  • PointNot much, but there's … a few streets away.
  • WhyIt's hardly …, but early on … it's … enough to hear …
  • ExampleLast Sunday, for instance, I sat there with … and watched … I'd never noticed …
Model answer

PointNot much, but there's a small lake a few streets away. WhyIt's hardly wild, but early on a Sunday it's quiet enough to hear birds instead of motorbikes. ExampleLast Sunday, for instance, I sat there with my anatomy notes and watched a kingfisher dive into the water three times. I'd never noticed a single one in the city before.

6 · Did you spend much time outdoors when you were a child?

  • PointAll the time. I grew up in …, surrounded by …
  • WhyThere was no … at home, so … were our playground.
  • ExampleOne summer, for example, my cousin and I spent … trying to … We never …, but …
Model answer

PointAll the time. I grew up in a small village in the Red River delta, surrounded by rice fields. WhyThere was no internet at home, so the river and the fields were our playground. ExampleOne summer, for example, my cousin and I spent a week trying to catch a huge fish in the canal behind our house. We never caught it, but I learned to swim.

7 · Have you ever stayed somewhere far away from any towns?

  • PointYes, during our … in … last year.
  • WhyThe camp was …, so there was no …, no …, nothing.
  • ExampleOn the third night, for example, the … broke down, and I saw how dark … really is without … You could hear …, but …
Model answer

PointYes, during our summer field training in the hills west of Hà Nội last year. WhyThe camp was far away from any towns, so there was no shop, no phone signal, nothing. ExampleOn the third night, for example, the generator broke down, and I saw how dark a forest really is without a single light anywhere. You could hear insects everywhere, but you couldn't see your own hand.

Let's talk about photos, hopes and dreams.

Choose one card. Jot down key words for 1 minute, then talk for 2 minutes without stopping. Cover all three prompts and the last line, and add an idea of your own if there's time.

Cue card A · An extreme weather event or natural disaster (bank topic 7)
