  • WhyI've chosen it because it was the strongest typhoon to reach … in decades. More than … people died or went missing, and the damage from …, … and … came to over …
  • HowIt made landfall in … and … early on … afternoon, the …, and by evening the wind in … was the strongest I've ever felt. The next morning, …
  • ExampleBut the moment I'll never forget came … later, when a flash flood swept through …, a small village in …, and buried …
  • ResultDozens of people there …, and soldiers searched the area for … Afterwards, the army built … on safer ground, and families began moving in …
  • LimitationAdmittedly, I only saw the easy part, since in … we lost …, while families in … lost …
  • EvaluationI felt … during the storm itself, but the … feeling afterwards was much worse. If a storm like that came again, I'd want to be …, not …
Model answer · Cue card A · ≈ 240 words for a 2-minute talk

PointThe event I'm going to talk about is Typhoon Yagi, or Storm Number 3 as most of us called it, which hit the north in September 2024. I was in Hà Nội when it came through. WhyI've chosen it because it was the strongest typhoon to reach the north in decades. More than three hundred people died or went missing, and the damage from the wind, floods and landslides came to over eighty trillion đồng. HowIt made landfall in Quảng Ninh and Hải Phòng early on Saturday afternoon, the seventh, and by evening the wind in Hà Nội was the strongest I've ever felt. The next morning, there were fallen trees on every street around the academy. ExampleBut the moment I'll never forget came three days later, when a flash flood swept through Làng Nủ, a small village in Lào Cai, and buried most of its houses under mud. ResultDozens of people there lost their lives, and soldiers searched the area for two weeks. Afterwards, the army built forty new houses on safer ground, and families began moving in that December. LimitationAdmittedly, I only saw the easy part, since in Hà Nội we lost trees and power, while families in the mountains lost everything. EvaluationI felt scared during the storm itself, but the helpless feeling afterwards was much worse. If a storm like that came again, I'd want to be up there with a medical team, not reading about it on my phone.

3 prompts + the card's last line · 7 steps
Look again
  • Typhoon Yagi, or Storm Number 3 as most of us called it … — What the event was in the first breath: the international name, then the name people used at home
  • It made landfall in Quảng Ninh and Hải Phòng early on Saturday afternoon … — When and where it happened: a day and two places, then one thing you felt yourself (the wind in Hà Nội), so the facts become your story
  • … a flash flood swept through Làng Nủ, a small village in Lào Cai … — What damage it caused: one place told in detail stays with the listener longer than a list of provinces; Group 1 words carry it (a typhoon, damage, a flash flood)
  • Dozens of people there lost their lives … — a talk about a disaster stays calm and respectful: give places and numbers, leave out graphic details, and say what was rebuilt
  • … If a storm like that came again, I'd want to be up there … — explain how you felt: name the feeling, then imagine the next time with the second conditional (Sheet 4, Grammar 1: if + past simple, 'd + verb)

Cue card B · A wild animal you have seen (bank topic 8)

  • PointThe wild animal I'd like to describe is …, a rare … people here call the ‘…’. I saw … last summer.
  • WhyIt's worth talking about because it's a critically endangered species, and the biggest group left in Vietnam lives on …, a protected area next to … Nobody's sure how many there are, maybe …, maybe …
  • HowI was staying with … during my summer leave, and early one morning we rode … up the side of the mountain to a bend where …
  • ExampleAfter about an hour, a mother climbed down into …, with a baby clinging to … She looked as if she was dressed for …: a … body, … hands, white forearms like …, dark red … like …, and a … face with …
  • ResultWe didn't move or speak for …, and she just carried on … I took about … photos, and … were actually in focus.
  • LimitationAdmittedly, it wasn't exactly …, since there are … all over the peninsula now.
  • EvaluationEven so, I felt … and a little … If nobody protected …, there'd be nothing left for … except …, which is why …
Model answer · Cue card B · ≈ 240 words for a 2-minute talk

PointThe wild animal I'd like to describe is the red-shanked douc langur, a rare monkey people here call the ‘queen of primates’. I saw a family of them last summer. WhyIt's worth talking about because it's a critically endangered species, and the biggest group left in Vietnam lives on the Sơn Trà Peninsula, a protected area next to Đà Nẵng. Nobody's sure how many there are, maybe a few hundred, maybe thirteen hundred. HowI was staying with my aunt during my summer leave, and early one morning we rode her motorbike up the side of the mountain to a bend where a ranger said they often feed. ExampleAfter about an hour, a mother climbed down into a fig tree ten metres away, with a baby clinging to her chest. She looked as if she was dressed for a festival: a grey body, black hands, white forearms like long gloves, dark red lower legs like stockings, and a golden face with white whiskers. ResultWe didn't move or speak for twenty minutes, and she just carried on eating leaves. I took about a hundred photos, and two were actually in focus. LimitationAdmittedly, it wasn't exactly deep jungle, since there are roads and hotels all over the peninsula now. EvaluationEven so, I felt lucky and a little guilty. If nobody protected that forest, there'd be nothing left for our kids except pictures, which is why I now follow GreenViet, the local group that studies them.

3 prompts + the card's last line · 7 steps
Look again
  • … the red-shanked douc langur, a rare monkey people here call the ‘queen of primates’ … — What the animal is: its English name, a plain explanation (a rare monkey) and the local nickname
  • … early one morning we rode her motorbike up the side of the mountain … — Where and when you saw it in one sentence; the ranger's tip is the small detail that makes it sound true
  • She looked as if she was dressed for a festival: a grey body, black hands … — the card's line Why it looked like asks what it looked like: one comparison with as if, then the colours from top to toe so the listener can picture her
  • Nobody's sure how many there are, maybe a few hundred … — when the counts disagree, give the range and say so; nobody takes a positive verb (Nobody's sure, never Nobody isn't sure; Sheet 4, Grammar 2)
  • … If nobody protected that forest, there'd be nothing left … — how you felt comes first (lucky, a little guilty), then an imagined consequence: the second conditional with nobody and nothing, and no double negative

Preparing for extreme weather

HowA short checklist does the job: water, rice, a torch and charged power banks. ResultThe wind took half the roof off the house next door, but theirs stayed on, and those buckets got them through four days without tap water. LimitationAdmittedly, poorer families can't always afford to stock up, and some old people refuse to leave home. HowPeople also trust their eyes, and a bit of water on the road never looks dangerous. ExampleLast summer, for instance, during a flood warning in Hà Nội, I watched a man ride his motorbike into a flooded underpass because the car in front had made it. ResultHis engine died halfway, and two of us from the bus stop had to help him push it out of waist-deep water. LimitationThen again, some warnings cover a whole province, so nobody knows if their street is at risk. EvaluationSo warnings work best when they're local, like a text that names the streets to avoid.

Sheet 8 / 11 · Writing · the cause–effect paragraph · 9 stages

Writing: the cause–effect paragraph, frame by frame

After the opinion paragraph (11c–11d) and the advantages–disadvantages paragraph (11e–11f), this sheet trains the cause–effect paragraph: why something happens, what a real event does, and what would happen if something changed.

0 exercises checked
1 Master frames2 Topic sentence3 Cause / effect4 The chain5 Example + result6 Would7 Conclude8 Together9 Write

Stage 1 The three master frames

GoalLearn the bold words of Frames A, B and C and watch each one at work in a model paragraph beside it.
Why this worksThe frame carries the organisation, so attention is free for ideas and grammar; the later stages remove it one piece at a time.
Recap · the cause–effect paragraph on one card · 10 slots
  1. Topic sentence · topic + causes / effects + how many
  2. Cause / effect 1 · the first cause / effect
  3. The chain · because … so …
  4. Example · a real or typical case
  5. Result · what that case leads to
  6. Cause / effect 2 · a different cause / effect
  7. The chain · because … so …
  8. Example · a real or typical case
  9. Result · what that case leads to
  10. Concluding sentence · sum up / look ahead, nothing new
  • Before slot 1: look at the question word. Why …? asks for causes; What are the effects of …? asks what a real event does; What would happen if …? asks for imagined effects.
  • Three frames: A = two causes · B = what a real event does · C = what an imagined change would do: would in every effect and result and in the closing sentence; real facts and cases may stay present or past.
  • The chain: every cause or effect gets a because … so … sentence, one specific case and the result of that case.
  • The target: one block of 140–170 words (8–10 sentences) in formal English: no contractions, no you, no questions.
Know this
  • A frame = words that never change (in bold) + coloured gaps. The bold words organise the paragraph; the ideas in the gaps are yours.
  • Read the question first: Why …? → Frame A (causes) · the effects of something that really happens → Frame B · What would happen if …? → Frame C (imagined effects, second conditional).
  • The tabs change the frame and the model beside it at the same time: every model is its frame, filled in.
From the coursebook · SB p. 143, Exercise 7 · a mini Frame C paragraph
What would happen if there wasn’t a Gulf Stream?

The coursebook answers its own What would happen if …? question with a Frame C paragraph in miniature. You will read it, with its eight verb gaps, in Practice Exercise 7. This is how it is built:

  • Sentences 1–2 the real situation now: what the Gulf Stream is, and what it does for the climate of Europe (As a result, …).
  • Sentence 3 the imagined change: If + past simple, would + verb.
  • Sentences 4–6 the effects, each leading to the next: colder British winters → shorter springs and summers → less food from farms, dearer heating.
  • Sentence 7 So if …, … would …: what the change would mean for people.
  • Our paragraph the same job at B1+ length: two effects, each explained and proved.
Model paragraph for the tab you picked · frame words in bold

Model A · 169 words · 10 sentences

Why do many people who live in big cities rarely notice nature?

1There are two main reasons why many city people rarely notice the natural world around them. 2The first reason is that city life keeps most people indoors and in a hurry. 3This means that their eyes stay on the traffic or a screen, so they miss what grows by the road. 4For example, the US Environmental Protection Agency estimates that Americans spend about 90 percent of their time indoors. 5As a result, city trees, birds and insects become a background nobody sees. 6Another reason is that many people imagine nature as big, wild and far away. 7Because of this picture, they ignore the small living things in a park or a crack in the pavement. 8For instance, the photographer David Liittschwager found plenty to photograph inside a one-cubic-foot frame in Central Park. 9This is why his photos surprise so many city people, who believe they have to travel to see wildlife. 10In short, indoor routines and a narrow idea of nature hide the life on their doorstep.

Model B · 169 words · 10 sentences

What are the effects of a serious flood on a small town?

1A serious flood has two lasting effects on a small town. 2The first effect is that many families lose their homes and their income at the same time. 3This happens because the water ruins houses, shops and crops together, so people lose the money they need for repairs. 4For example, in October 2020, the Kiến Giang River in Lệ Thủy, then part of Quảng Bình province, rose almost a metre above its 1979 record. 5As a result, thousands of families there depended on outside help for weeks. 6Another serious effect is on people's health. 7Dirty floodwater gets into wells and homes, which leads to stomach illnesses, skin infections and, a few weeks later, more mosquitoes. 8For instance, a small health station may see long queues of patients with infected cuts once the water goes down. 9This means that local doctors and nurses are often at their busiest just when their own homes need repairing. 10In short, a flood damages both the wealth and the health of a small town.

Model C · 169 words · 10 sentences

What would happen if heavy snow fell in Hà Nội every winter?

1If heavy snow fell in Hà Nội every winter, two important things would happen to life in the city. 2First, daily travel would become slow and dangerous. 3This would happen because the city has no snowploughs, and millions of motorbikes would slide on icy roads. 4For example, when snow fell in Sa Pa in January 2016, ice on the Ô Quy Hồ Pass made driving dangerous. 5As a result, many workers and students in a snowy Hà Nội would stay at home on the worst days. 6Second, the cold would put people's health at greater risk. 7The reason is that most homes in Hà Nội are built for hot summers, so they would lose heat fast in freezing weather. 8For instance, an elderly couple without heating would struggle to keep warm and might develop a chest infection. 9This would mean longer queues at big hospitals such as Bạch Mai every winter. 10In short, regular snow would make Hà Nội slower to move around and riskier for its oldest residents.

The model here follows the tab you pick on the right.

The master frames · bold words stay, coloured gaps are yours

Frame A · two causes · for a Why …? question

  1. Topic sentence · topic + causes / effects + how manyThere are two main reasons why something happens ….In model A: sentence 1
  2. Cause / effect 1 · cause 1The first reason is that cause 1 ….In model A: sentence 2
  3. The chain · because … so …This means that how it leads on …, so the next step ….In model A: sentence 3
  4. Example · a real or typical caseFor example, a real case ….In model A: sentence 4
  5. Result · what that case leads toAs a result, what follows ….In model A: sentence 5
  6. Cause / effect 2 · cause 2Another reason is that cause 2 ….In model A: sentence 6
  7. The chain · because … so …Because of a noun …, what happens ….In model A: sentence 7
  8. Example · a real or typical caseFor instance, a named case ….In model A: sentence 8
  9. Result · back to the questionThis is why the effect in the question ….In model A: sentence 9
  10. Concluding sentence · both causes, new wordsIn short, both causes in new words ….In model A: sentence 10

Frame B · the effects of a real event, for What are the effects of …?

  1. Topic sentence · topic + causes / effects + how manya real event … has two lasting effects on who / what ….In model B: sentence 1
  2. Cause / effect 1 · effect 1The first effect is that effect 1 ….In model B: sentence 2
  3. The chain · because … so …This happens because the cause …, so what follows ….In model B: sentence 3
  4. Example · a real or typical caseFor example, in a month and a year …, what happened ….In model B: sentence 4
  5. Result · what that case leads toAs a result, what follows ….In model B: sentence 5
  6. Cause / effect 2 · effect 2Another serious effect is on a noun ….In model B: sentence 6
  7. The chain · because … so …what happens …, which leads to a noun ….In model B: sentence 7
  8. Example · a real or typical caseFor instance, a typical case ….In model B: sentence 8
  9. Result · what that case leads toThis means that what follows ….In model B: sentence 9
  10. Concluding sentence · both effects, new wordsIn short, both effects in new words ….In model B: sentence 10

Frame C · an imagined change, for What would happen if …? The past simple after If, then would / could / might in every effect, every result and the last sentence.

  1. Topic sentence · the imagined change + two effectsIf past simple …, two important things would happen to whom ….In model C: sentence 1
  2. Cause / effect 1 · imagined effect 1First, someone / something … would verb ….In model C: sentence 2
  3. The chain · because … so …This would happen because a real fact …, and what would follow ….In model C: sentence 3
  4. Example · a real or typical caseFor example, when a real case …, what happened ….In model C: sentence 4
  5. Result · what that case leads toAs a result, someone … would verb ….In model C: sentence 5
  6. Cause / effect 2 · imagined effect 2Second, someone / something … would verb ….In model C: sentence 6
  7. The chain · because … so …The reason is that a real fact …, so someone … would verb ….In model C: sentence 7
  8. Example · a real or typical caseFor instance, a typical case … would verb ….In model C: sentence 8
  9. Result · what that case leads toThis would mean what follows ….In model C: sentence 9
  10. Concluding sentence · both effects, still with wouldIn short, both effects … would verb ….In model C: sentence 10
Stage 1a

Model C: what job does each of sentences 2–9 do?

Sentence 1 opens the paragraph and sentence 10 closes it. The model on the left changes to Model C.
2Sentence 2 =
First, … would … opens the first imagined effect: travel turns slow and dangerous. It is an effect of the snow, not a cause.
3Sentence 3 =
This would happen because gives the links behind it: no snowploughs → motorbikes sliding on ice.
4Sentence 4 =
For example, when … + one real case: Sa Pa, January 2016, ice on a mountain pass.
5Sentence 5 =
As a result, says what that case would lead to in Hà Nội: people late or stuck at home.
6Sentence 6 =
Second, opens the second imagined effect, on health.
7Sentence 7 =
The reason is that … so … links homes built for summer to rooms that lose heat.
8Sentence 8 =
For instance, + one typical case: an elderly couple with no heating.
9Sentence 9 =
This would mean takes the chain one step further: longer hospital queues.
Stage 1b

Which type of paragraph would each first sentence begin?

Sentence 1 tells the reader which frame is coming. Two of the six do not open a cause–effect paragraph at all.
1Cadets often feel exhausted in their first month of field training for two main reasons.
→
for two main reasons promises causes: Frame A.
2Last September's storm hurt the fishing villages on the coast in two lasting ways.
→
A real event that has already happened + the two lasting ways it hurt the villages: Frame B.
3Moving the academy to a new campus in the mountains would change cadet life in two big ways.
→
would change … in two big ways: an imagined change and its effects → Frame C.
4Doing night shifts as a student brings real benefits as well as some clear drawbacks.
→
Benefits and drawbacks are the two sides of an advantages–disadvantages paragraph, the type of Unit 11e–11f.
5Road accidents in the rainy season are mainly caused by poor visibility and slippery surfaces.
→
are mainly caused by + two causes: Frame A in another form.
6Flooding in city streets could be reduced by two practical measures.
→
could be reduced by … measures promises solutions, not causes or effects: a problem–solution paragraph.
Stage 1c

Other frame words for the same job: which could replace the bold words?

Find the frame words that could do the same job. Stages 2–7 add more of them.
1Model A · sentence 2 · The first reason is that … →
Both open the first cause. effect would turn the paragraph round, and reason is because says the reason twice (write is that).
2Model A · sentence 9 · This is why … →
Both lead from the cause forward to the effect in the question. This is because runs the other way, from an effect back to its cause.
3Model B · sentence 3 · This happens because … →
Both give the cause behind the effect. The result of this and This is why point forward to a result; Because of needs a noun.
4Model B · sentence 6 · Another serious effect is on … →
Both add a second effect + on + a noun. cause changes the job, and The first cannot follow an effect already given.
5Model C · sentence 5 · As a result, … →
Both introduce a result + a full sentence. Because would turn the sentence into a cause; However would bring a contrast.
6Model C · sentence 10 · In short, … →
Both open the last sentence and gather the two effects together.

Stage 2 Topic-sentence frames

GoalOpen with a sentence that names the topic, promises causes or effects, and gives their number.
Why this worksSentence 1 is a promise: it tells the reader which frame is coming, and a body that answers a different question loses marks for task response.
Topic-sentence frames
  1. There are two main reasons why something happens ….Frame A
  2. the problem … is mainly caused by cause 1 … and cause 2 ….Frame A
  3. a real event … has two serious effects on who / what ….Frame B
  4. a real event … can affect who / what … in two important ways.Frame B
  5. If past simple …, two important things would happen.Frame C
  6. an imagined change … would have two major effects on who / what ….Frame C
  • Topic + controlling idea: causes or effects, and how many (two).
  • reasons why + subject + verb, in statement order: why cities flood, never why do cities flood.
  • an effect on + noun (the noun) · affect + noun (the verb).
  • Frame C: If + past simple, then would + verb; never would straight after If.
  • Avoid: This paragraph will talk about … · The reason why … is because …
Stage 2a

Build a topic sentence from notes, part by part

Read the notes first; then choose the parts of the frame from left to right.
Why do many young people rarely spend time in nature?
Notes

Frame A, effect first · the effect: young people and nature · two causes

people is already plural and takes many, not much; no of or the when you mean young people in general. people is plural (spend); rarely goes before the main verb; nature in general has no the. .The other Frame A form: the effect first, then for two main reasons (a plural noun after two; effects would promise the wrong thing).

What would happen if cars were banned from the city centre one day a week?
Notes

Frame C · the imagined change: cars banned from the city centre one day a week · two effects

If opens an imagined condition. Whether introduces a choice, not a condition; Unless means the opposite. An imagined change takes the past after If (here the passive were banned); never would or will in the if-clause. .A comma after the if-clause, then would + the base verb (follow) and a plural noun after two.

Stage 2b

Which topic sentence matches the writer’s plan?

1 · Why do many young people rarely spend time in nature?
The writer’s plan

cause 1: long hours of study and part-time work · cause 2: few green places near home

Which topic sentence matches the writer’s plan?
C names the two causes in the plan. A promises effects the plan never gives, B is too broad to prove, D is an announcement.
2 · What are the effects of a hailstorm on farms?
The writer’s plan

effect 1: crops torn apart in minutes · effect 2: roofs and greenhouses broken

Which topic sentence matches the writer’s plan?
B names the effects of a real event and says how many. A promises causes, C mixes fell with will and names one vague feeling, D is a definition.
3 · What would happen if every student had to grow one plant?
The writer’s plan

effect 1: students would understand how plants live and grow · effect 2: the school would look greener

Which topic sentence matches the writer’s plan?
D keeps the change imagined (would bring) and promises two effects. A uses the real (first) conditional and names one effect, B has no proper verb, C is a fact that promises nothing.
Stage 2c

Repair the topic sentence

One underlined part in each sentence is wrong. Choose what should replace it.
1The two main reasons why do so many cadets skip breakfast are a lack of time and a poor appetite early in the morning.
→
After reasons why, statement order (no do): why so many cadets skip breakfast.
2A long drought can have two serious affects on rice farmers.
→
After two serious a plural noun is needed: effects. Affect is the verb.
3If every cadet would have a bicycle, the campus would be quieter.
→
No would after If: the past simple had carries the imagined meaning.
4The reason why many roads flood is because the drains are blocked.
→
The reason why … is that + a clause; reason and because would say the same thing twice.
5A sudden hailstorm can effect a whole village in two ways.
→
After can a verb is needed: affect. Effect is the noun.
6If the city planted a tree outside every school, two good things will happen.
→
An imagined change (planted) needs would + the base verb in the result.

Your topic sentence

What would happen if there were no parks or trees in big cities?

Write your topic sentence with a Frame C line from the card: the imagined change + two effects.

Two models

1Without parks or trees, our cities would face two worrying problems.

2A city with no green spaces at all would have two major effects on the health of its people.

Stage 3 Cause and effect frames

GoalIntroduce cause or effect 1 and cause or effect 2 with frames that show their order and their job.
Why this worksSignposts let a reader count the points, and the right forms (a cause of, an effect on, the reason is that) remove the commonest class errors.
Cause and effect frames
  1. The first reason is that cause 1 ….cause 1 · Frame A
  2. One major cause of the problem … is a noun / V-ing ….cause 1 · Frame A
  3. Another reason is that cause 2 ….cause 2 · Frame A
  4. The first effect is that effect 1 ….effect 1 · Frame B
  5. Another serious effect is on a noun ….effect 2 · Frame B
  6. First, someone / something … would verb …. Second, …effects 1 and 2 · Frame C
  • A cause or an effect is general: say what happens. Names, years and places wait for the example.
  • Cause 2 (or effect 2) is a different one, not cause 1 in new words.
  • a cause of + noun · an effect on + noun · the reason is that + a clause (never is because).
  • Frame C: would in every effect (First, … would …), never will.
Stage 3a

Pick the opening frame for each slot

The coloured tag names the slot. Every option is a frame; the words after the … complete the sentence.
1Cause 1Why do many young people rarely spend time in nature? school and work leave them very little free time in daylight.
It opens the first cause: The first reason is that + a clause. Another needs a cause before it, is because is a class mistake, and effect is the wrong job.
2Cause 2Why do many young people rarely spend time in nature? parks and forests can feel far away from their homes and dormitories.
A second, different cause: Another reason (singular after another). This is because would make it a chain sentence; effect changes the job.
3Effect 1What are the effects of a hailstorm on farms? young plants can be torn to pieces in minutes.
The first effect, with is that + a clause. affect is a verb, cause is the wrong job, and Another needs an effect before it.
4Effect 2What are the effects of a heatwave on people's health? the way people sleep.
effect on + a noun phrase (the way people sleep). affect is a verb, is that on mixes two patterns, and reason is the wrong job.
5Cause 1Why do big cities flood so often after heavy rain? the loss of open ground that once soaked up the rain.
a cause of + noun, then is + a noun phrase (the loss of …). effect turns the idea round; one of the needs a plural noun.
6Effect 1 · Frame CWhat would happen if every student had to grow one plant? learn how much care a living thing needs.
An imagined effect: would + the base verb. will is for a real future, would to is never correct, and If students would puts would in the if-clause.
Stage 3b

From a note to a cause or an effect: note → frame → sentence

Each note is in Vietnamese (the Dinh Thang method). Choose the English a native writer would write.
1 · Why do many young people rarely spend time in nature?
Note → frame

một nguyên nhân chính là giới trẻ dành quá nhiều thời gian cho điện thoại · frame: One main cause is that …

Which sentence is natural English?
A: is that + a clause, too much time on. B drops that and says too many time for, C uses is because, D keeps the Vietnamese word order.
2 · What are the effects of a heatwave on people's health?
Note → frame

một tác động khác là người cao tuổi dễ bị mất nước · frame: Another effect is that …

Which sentence is natural English?
D: bị mất nước = become dehydrated, and dễ = more easily. A translates word for word, B uses the verb affect as a noun, C drops is that and says easy to be.
3 · What would happen if cars were banned from the city centre one day a week?
Note → frame

nếu cấm ô tô, trẻ em sẽ có chỗ chơi an toàn hơn · frame: If … would …

Which sentence is natural English?
C: the past after If (were banned), then would have + safer places to play. A is the real conditional with more safe place, B puts would in the if-clause, D has no subject after If.

Effect 1

What would happen if there were no parks or trees in big cities?

Write the first effect of a city with no parks or trees, opening with a Frame C effect frame (would).

Two models

1The first thing that would happen is that city streets would turn into ovens every summer.

2One major effect would be on the quality of the air in busy streets.

Stage 4 Chain frames

GoalAfter each cause or effect, show how one thing leads to the next (because … so …).
Why this worksCause–effect writing is judged by its links; a point with no chain behind it stays a claim.
Chain frames · how one thing leads to the next
  1. This is because the cause behind it ….why it happens
  2. This happens because the cause …, so what follows ….the chain · Frames A and B
  3. This would happen because a real fact …, so what would follow ….the chain · Frame C
  4. When the cause …, the effect …, which leads to a noun ….a longer chain
  5. Because of a noun …, the effect …. · Due to a noun …, …the cause as a noun
  6. In other words, the point, said more clearly ….what it really means
  • Show the chain: cause → effect → the next effect. One link alone is only a claim.
  • because + a clause · because of / due to + a noun · so + a clause · lead to + a noun or V-ing.
  • Keep the direction right: the cause goes after because, the effect after so and which leads to.
Stage 4a

Complete each chain with the frame that fits

Look at what follows the gap (a clause? a noun?), then decide: a cause, a meaning, or a link in an imagined chain.
1What are the effects of a hailstorm on farms?
Point

Hail can ruin a field of vegetables in a few minutes.

hailstones fall at high speed and tear the leaves apart.
A whole clause (subject + verb) follows, so This is because. Because of and Due to need a noun; This is why points the wrong way, to a result.
2Why do many young people rarely spend time in nature?
Point

On weekdays, most students hardly see a tree.

long hours of study and work, they leave home early and come back after dark.
A noun phrase follows (long hours of study and work), so Because of. Because would need a clause; So and This is why would turn the cause into a result.
3What are the effects of a heatwave on people's health?
Point

Hot weather can be dangerous for older people.

their bodies sweat less as they age, so they find it harder to cool down.
This happens because + a clause, then so carries the chain on. because of needs a noun; This is why turns it into a result.
4What would happen if cars were banned from the city centre one day a week?
Point

A car-free day would make the centre quieter.

engines and horns would disappear from its streets for a whole day.
Frame C keeps would: This would happen because + a clause. will leaves the imagined world; because of needs a noun.
5Why do big cities flood so often after heavy rain?
Point

Rubbish makes city floods worse.

plastic bags and bottles block the drains that should carry the water away.
In other words restates the point in plainer, fuller words. In other word is a mistake, Another reason starts a new cause, and Due to / As a result of need a noun.
Stage 4b

A list or a chain? Choose the sentence that links the point to what follows

The weakest cause–effect paragraphs list points with no because or so after any of them.
1 · Why do big cities flood so often after heavy rain?
Point · a cause

Concrete and asphalt now cover most of the ground in big cities.

Which next sentence shows how this leads to floods?
C shows the chain: hard ground → no soaking → all the water in the drains at once. A lists a new point, B defines a word, D is personal.
2 · What are the effects of a hailstorm on farms?
Point · an effect

Hail can break the roofs of farm buildings.

Which sentence should come next to explain it?
A says why roofs break so easily (thin sheets and tiles). B lists a new effect, C defines a word, D is a vague example.
3 · What would happen if every student had to grow one plant?
Point · an imagined effect

Students would become more patient.

Which sentence would explain this point?
B keeps would and shows the chain: slow growth → weeks of care → patience. A lists a new point, C says nothing new, D slips into will and stops after one link.
Your turn · main task

The chain

What would happen if there were no parks or trees in big cities?

Write the chain behind your first effect, keeping would: how does one thing lead to the next?

A model

1This would happen because concrete and asphalt soak up the sun's heat all day and give it back at night, so streets without shade would hardly cool down.

Stage 5 Example and result frames

GoalProve each point with one specific case, real or typical, then say what that case leads to.
Why this worksA real place, a date or a name persuades better than many people, and the result adds the final link of the chain.
Example and result frames
  1. For example, in a year …, what happened ….example · a real event
  2. For instance, a typical case ….example
  3. For example, if a case …, someone … would verb ….example · Frame C
  4. As a result, what follows ….result
  5. This leads to a noun / V-ing …. · This would lead to …result
  6. This is why the effect in the question ….result · back to the question (Frame A)
  7. This would mean that what would follow ….result · Frame C
  • Example: a real case (a place, a year, a name) or a typical case (a farmer in Lào Cai may …); always reasonable: no invented percentages, no my uncle says.
  • Result: what follows from THAT case, one more link in the chain.
  • lead to + a noun or V-ing · As a result, + a full sentence · As a result of + a noun.
Stage 5a

Which ending makes a good example?

The frame opens the sentence; choose how it ends.
1 · Why do big cities flood so often after heavy rain?
Point · a cause

When too much of a city is paved, heavy rain has nowhere to go but the streets.

Frame: For example, in … Which ending finishes the frame and supports the point?
B: a month, a year, a real place and what the rain did there. A is vague, C is true but says nothing about rain, D invents a figure.
2 · What are the effects of a heatwave on people's health?
Point · an effect

Extreme heat is especially dangerous for older people who live alone.

Frame: For instance, … Which ending finishes the frame and supports the point?
D: one typical person, a place and what happens to her. A is vague, B is true but proves nothing, C is personal.
3 · What would happen if cars were banned from the city centre one day a week?
Point · an imagined effect

Without cars, the streets of the centre would become safer for walkers and cyclists.

Frame: For example, if … Which ending finishes the frame and supports the point?
A: one typical imagined case, past simple + could. B says nothing, C slips into the real conditional (bans … will), D is personal.
Stage 5b

What does the example lead to?

Each grey line is an example; choose the sentence that says what it leads to.
1ExampleFor instance, a cadet who spends a whole weekend scrolling through videos in the dormitory may never step outside.→
It follows from THAT case. Thanks to this brings good news only, As a result of needs a noun, phones are expensive opens a new point and the campus has many trees is one more example.
2ExampleFor example, during a long heatwave, a construction worker may keep working at midday because he is paid by the day.→
lead to + a noun (heatstroke). A bare verb cannot follow lead to; fitter and stronger is the wrong result, As a result of, is broken, and In short ends the paragraph.
3ExampleFor example, if a snowstorm hit Hà Nội on a Monday morning, buses would be stuck on icy bridges.→
Frame C stays imagined: would + the base verb. will leaves the imagined world, would missed is wrong, early patients do not follow from a traffic jam, and the colour of snow is off the point.
4ExampleFor example, a student who grew up in a city flat may never have walked through a real forest.→
What follows from never having been in a forest: it feels strange. more relaxing than any flat says the opposite, lead to feel needs a noun after lead to, and the sentences about trees and natural places go off the point.
Your turn · main task

Example + result

What would happen if there were no parks or trees in big cities?

Write a case for your first effect, then its result: two sentences, with would wherever the case is imagined.

A model

1For example, a market seller who works all day on a treeless pavement would feel the full force of the midday sun. As a result, she might have to stop work for hours or risk fainting.

Stage 6 Second-conditional frames (Frame C)

GoalKeep every effect, every result and the final sentence of a What would happen if …? paragraph in the imagined world.
Why this worksOne slip into will or a present verb tells the reader the change is real; the grammar of Unit 12a is the backbone of Frame C.
Second-conditional frames · Frame C
  1. If past simple …, someone … would verb ….the imagined change + an effect
  2. someone … would verb … if past simple ….the same, with no comma
  3. Without a noun …, someone … would verb ….a short if-clause
  4. someone … could verb … · someone … might verb ….would be able to · would perhaps
  5. This would mean that what would follow ….result
  6. If subject … were adjective / noun …, …formal: were for every person
  • In the if-clause, the past simple (had, were, lived); in the result, would + the base verb.
  • Stay in the imagined world: every effect, result and the last sentence keep would / could / might; no will.
  • A real fact or a real case may back up the idea in the present or the past (trees shade streets, in 2016 …).
  • If-clause first → a comma before the result; if in the middle → no comma.
Stage 6a

Choose the form that keeps the paragraph imagined

Every sentence comes from a What would happen if …? paragraph. Choose the verb form for the gap.
1What would happen if every student had to grow one plant?If every classroom a row of plants, the corridors would soon look greener.
The if-clause takes the past simple (had); never would or will after If.
2Students which plants need sun and which prefer shade.
An imagined effect: would + the base verb.
3A careless student kill a plant in a week, but even that mistake would teach something.
might = would perhaps: a possible imagined effect. will and is going to are real futures; would to and may will are never correct.
4What would happen if cars were banned from the city centre one day a week?If there no cars in the centre on Sundays, street sellers could use the road.
Formal English uses were after If for every person; would be and will be cannot go in the if-clause.
5Bus companies add extra buses every Sunday.
would have to = an imagined duty. would must does not exist, and would had to doubles the past.
6Without traffic, people hear birds in the trees around the lake.
could = would be able to; will can and would can do not exist.
Stage 6b

Spot the slip out of the imagined world

Each underlined part breaks the second conditional. Choose the repair.
1If the city would close the centre to traffic, buses would run on time.
→
No would straight after If: the past simple closed.
2If every student grew a plant, the school will look much greener.
→
The if-clause is imagined (grew), so the result needs would + the base verb.
3Without cars for a day, the centre is a safer place for children.
→
Without cars … is an imagined condition, so the result stays imagined: would be.
4If the drains were bigger the streets would stay dry after a storm.
→
When the if-clause comes first, a comma follows it; past were, not would be; bigger, not more big.
5If cadets had more free weekends, they would went hiking more often.
→
would + the base verb: would go.
Your turn · main task

Effect 2 + its chain

What would happen if there were no parks or trees in big cities?

Write your second effect and its chain, with would (or could / might) in both sentences.

Two models

1Second, children would lose most of their safe places to play outdoors. If there were no parks, they would spend even more of their free time indoors with screens.

2In addition, many birds and insects would vanish from the city, because they would have nowhere left to feed or nest.

Stage 7 Concluding frames

GoalClose by summing up both causes or effects, or by looking ahead: nothing new.
Why this worksThe last sentence is the one a reader remembers, and a new idea there is left unproved.
Concluding frames
  1. In short, both causes / effects in new words ….Frames A, B and C
  2. For these reasons, the effect in the question ….Frame A · sums up the causes
  3. Overall, the event … affects who … both effect 1 … and effect 2 ….Frame B
  4. In short, if past simple …, who … would verb ….Frame C
  5. If nothing changes, the effect … will continue / get worse ….looks ahead · Frames A and B
  • Sum up the two causes or effects, or look ahead; never a new cause, a new example or advice (… should also …).
  • Frame C stays imagined to the end: would, not will.
  • New words for the same ideas: do not copy the topic sentence.
Stage 7a

Choose the best concluding sentence

1 · Why do many young people rarely spend time in nature?
Topic sentence · Frame A

Young people today rarely get out into nature, and two causes stand out: busy timetables and a lack of nearby green space.

Which concluding sentence is best?
C sums up both causes in new words. A adds advice, B says nothing, D contradicts the topic sentence.
2 · What are the effects of a heatwave on people's health?
Topic sentence · Frame B

Heatwaves damage health in two ways: they overheat the body, and they make long-term illnesses worse.

Which concluding sentence is best?
A sums up both effects. B adds advice, C defines the topic, D turns from effects to causes.
3 · What would happen if cars were banned from the city centre one day a week?
Topic sentence · Frame C

A weekly car-free day in the city centre would bring two big changes for the people who use it.

Which concluding sentence is best?
B sums up both imagined effects and keeps would. A slips into will, C adds a new idea, D says nothing.
Stage 7b

Sums up, looks ahead, adds, mixes up or says nothing?

Six possible last sentences for one paragraph: three of them do the job.
What are the effects of a hailstorm on farms?
Topic sentence · Frame B

Hailstorms damage farms in two serious ways: they destroy crops and they wreck buildings.

1In short, a single hailstorm can wipe out both a season's harvest and the shelter a farm depends on.
→
Both effects (crops, buildings) in new words.
2If nothing changes, mountain farmers will keep losing crops and roofs to every spring storm.
→
It looks ahead from the same two effects and adds nothing new.
3Overall, farmers should also grow more fruit trees.
→
Fruit trees and advice were never part of the paragraph.
4In short, hail forms when strong storms carry raindrops high into freezing air.
→
The paragraph was about effects; this sentence suddenly explains what causes hail.
5Overall, hail is ice that falls from the sky.
→
True, but it sums up nothing.
6Overall, hail hurts a farm twice: once in the fields and again in the yard.
→
Fields (the crops) and the yard (the buildings): both effects, said a new way.
Your turn · main task

Sum it up

What would happen if there were no parks or trees in big cities?

Write your concluding sentence: sum up both effects and keep would; nothing new.

Two models

1Overall, losing every park and tree would make city life hotter, more stressful and much less healthy.

2In short, if cities lost their green spaces, the people living in them would pay with their comfort and their health.

Stage 8 Put the frame together

GoalFill in the frame words of a whole Frame C paragraph, then put a jumbled Frame B paragraph back in order.
Why this worksWatching all ten slots work in two complete paragraphs is the bridge to writing one alone in Stage 9.
The frames at a glance · A and B · C = What would happen if …?
  1. There are two main reasons why … / … has two serious effects on …C If …, two important things would happen.
  2. The first reason is that … / The first effect is that …C First, … would …
  3. This is because … / This happens because …, so …C This would happen because …
  4. For example, in year …, … / For example, …C For example, if …, … would …
  5. As a result, … / This leads to …C As a result, … would …
  6. Another reason is that … / Another serious effect is on …C Second, … would …
  7. Because of a noun …, … / … , which leads to …C The reason is that …, so … would …
  8. For instance, …C For instance, … would / might …
  9. This is why … / This means that …C This would mean that …
  10. In short, … / For these reasons, …C In short, if …, … would …
  • All ten slots sit in a single block of 140–170 words.
  • The frame words tell the reader what job the next sentence does.
  • Frame C: each effect, each result and the closing sentence take would; a real fact or case keeps its own tense.
Stage 8a

A whole Frame C paragraph: choose the frame words

A Frame C paragraph with ten gaps, one per slot: topic sentence · effect 1 · the chain · example · result · effect 2 · the chain · example · result · sum-up.
What would happen if cars were banned from the city centre one day a week?

Frame C · two imagined effects

(1) Without + a noun works like a short if-clause (If there were no cars …). With says the opposite; If, Unless, Although and Because need a full clause. cars in the centre for one day each week, the area would change in two clear ways. (2) It opens effect 1; the others bring a contrast, an example, the end or a cause. the air in its streets would become cleaner on that day. (3) A whole clause follows, and would keeps the change imagined; because of needs a noun and This is why points to a result. far fewer engines would be burning fuel in its narrow roads. (4) A real case (Paris, 2015) backs up the imagined effect; Such as cannot start a sentence. on the first car-free day in Paris, in September 2015, nitrogen dioxide in parts of the city fell by up to 40 percent. (5) What cleaner air would lead to: easier breathing. As a result of needs a noun. people with asthma would find it easier to breathe on car-free days. (6) Effect 2 follows effect 1: Second,. the streets would belong to people instead of traffic. (7) The reason is that + a clause gives the chain behind effect 2; is because is a class mistake and The result is that points the wrong way. families would feel safe enough to walk, cycle and let their children run in the road. (8) A specific case: the walking streets around Hoàn Kiếm Lake. the walking streets around Hoàn Kiếm Lake already fill with families every weekend evening. (9) The result stays imagined: would + the base verb (mean). small shops and cafés along the closed streets might gain more customers. (10) Overall opens the sum-up of both effects. closing the centre to cars once a week would make it a calmer and healthier place for everyone.

Stage 8b

Number the ten sentences in the right order (1–10)

The frame words at the start of each sentence are your clues. The answer key puts the sentences in order and highlights those clues.
What are the effects of a hailstorm on farms?

Frame B · effects of a real event

As a result, many families there lost the harvest they had planned to live on that season.
Result of the example: what the ruined fields meant for families.
The first effect is on the crops, which can be ruined at once.
Effect 1: The first effect is on opens the first point.
The reason is that big hailstones can smash the plastic covers of greenhouses and injure animals kept outside.
The chain behind effect 2: why buildings and animals suffer.
For example, in late March 2013, one hailstorm damaged fields of crops across several districts of Lào Cai.
Example of effect 1: one real storm, a date and a province.
Even a short hailstorm can do two kinds of serious damage to a farm.
Topic sentence: a real kind of event + two kinds of serious damage, so it opens a Frame B paragraph.
This means that money saved for seeds or school fees has to be spent on repairs instead.
Result of the example: This = the broken roofs.
Another effect is that homes, farm buildings and animals are hurt as well.
Effect 2: Another effect opens the second point.
In short, a few minutes of hail can cost a farming family both its harvest and its savings.
Concluding sentence: both effects (harvest, savings) in new words.
This happens because hard balls of ice tear the leaves and snap the stems.
The chain behind effect 1: how the ice ruins the crops.
For instance, the same storm tore the roofs off hundreds of houses in Mường Khương District.
Example of effect 2: the same storm points back to sentence 4, so it must come after it.

Stage 9 Write it with the frame

GoalWrite one paragraph per frame, with the help shrinking each time: a guided frame, then starters, then a free, timed task.
Why this worksSupport that is taken away step by step (gradual release) ends in independent writing, and at Level 1 even the weakest writer finishes a correct paragraph.
Know this
  • Level 1 · Guided frame (Frame A, why big cities flood): every box starts with its frame. A click on an idea fills the next gap (…); your own words work too.
  • Level 2 · Starters only (Frame B, a heatwave and health): the grey starter is a hint; the notes are ideas, and the sentences are yours.
  • Level 3 · Free and timed (Frame C, the main task): pick a topic-sentence frame, then write; 20 minutes.
  • Your paragraph shows everything you write, coloured slot by slot; Send to the writing box puts it in the Stage 9d box, ready for Self-check.
Stage 9a

Level 1 · Guided frame: Frame A, with the frame already in each box

Click an idea and it drops into the … of its box, or type your own words. The ideas alone give a paragraph of 143–169 words; then change a few words so that it sounds like you. Stuck? Show a model sits under every box.
Why do big cities flood so often after heavy rain?
1Topic sentence·topic + causes / effects + how many
the problem … for two main reasons.
Ideas

Big cities flood easily after heavy rain for two main reasons.

2Cause / effect 1·the first cause / effect
One main reason is that cause 1 ….
Ideas

One main reason is that most of the city is covered with roads, roofs and pavements.

3The chain·because … so …
This means that the chain, with so ….
Ideas

This means that rainwater cannot sink into the ground, so it pours into the drains all at once.

4Example·a real or typical case
For example, a real or typical case ….
Ideas

For example, a heavy afternoon downpour can leave streets in central Hồ Chí Minh City under water within an hour.

5Result·what that case leads to
As a result, what follows ….
Ideas

As a result, many people are late for work, and some motorbikes break down in the water.

6Cause / effect 2·a different cause / effect
A second cause is that cause 2 ….
Ideas

A second cause is that many lakes and ponds have been filled in to build houses and roads.

7The chain·because … so …
In other words, the point, said more clearly ….
Ideas

In other words, the places that used to store rainwater during a storm have disappeared.

8Example·a real or typical case
For instance, a typical case ….
Ideas

For instance, new housing estates are often built on low rice fields that used to flood safely.

9Result·what that case leads to
This is why the effect in the question ….
Ideas

This is why the same streets flood again every rainy season.

10Concluding sentence·sum up / look ahead, nothing new
In short, both causes in new words ….
Ideas

In short, paved ground and lost lakes leave heavy rain with nowhere to go.

Stage 9b

Level 2 · Starters only: Frame B, two effects of a real event

Each box shows a grey starter as a hint, and the notes under it are ideas, not sentences. Look at a model only after writing, to compare.
What are the effects of a heatwave on people's health?
1Topic sentence·topic + causes / effects + how many
  • Frame B · a real event
  • a heatwave · health

A heatwave can harm people's health in two serious ways.

2Cause / effect 1·the first cause / effect
  • the body · cannot cool down

The most immediate effect is that the body struggles to cool down.

3The chain·because … so …
  • sweating alone is not enough
  • temperature rises → heatstroke

This happens because sweating alone cannot cool the body in extreme heat, so its temperature keeps rising towards heatstroke.

4Example·a real or typical case
  • August 2003 · France
  • about 15,000 extra deaths · mostly older people

For example, in August 2003, a heatwave in France was linked to about 15,000 extra deaths, mostly among older people.

5Result·what that case leads to
  • France · a national heatwave plan · the next year

As a result, France set up a national heatwave warning plan the following year.

6Cause / effect 2·a different cause / effect
  • people with long-term illnesses

A second serious effect is on people who already have a long-term illness.

7The chain·because … so …
  • the body works hard to stay cool
  • heart pumps faster → strain

When the body works hard to stay cool, the heart must pump faster, which is dangerous for anyone with heart disease.

8Example·a real or typical case
  • a heart-failure patient · small room, metal roof
  • a week of extreme heat → hospital

For instance, a heart-failure patient in a room under a metal roof may need hospital care after a week of heat.

9Result·what that case leads to
  • hospitals fill up
  • staff also tired by the heat

This means that hospitals fill up during a heatwave, just when their staff are also struggling.

10Concluding sentence·sum up / look ahead, nothing new
  • directly · overheating
  • indirectly · weak hearts
  • new words

In short, extreme heat harms health directly by overheating the body and indirectly by pushing weak hearts past their limits.

Main task · one cause–effect paragraph (Frame C)What would happen if there were no parks or trees in big cities? Write one paragraph (140–170 words) about two effects, with would in each effect, each result and the conclusion.

Send your Level 3 boxes here, or type straight into the box: ten slots, one block of text.

Word count: 0 of 140–170 · 8–10 sentences, one block · 20′

Model paragraph · Frame C · 164 words · 10 sentences

Topic sentenceCause / effectThe chainExampleResultConcluding sentence

If big cities had no parks or trees, two serious things would happen to the people who live in them. First, city summers would become even hotter. This would happen because trees shade the streets and release water through their leaves, which cools the air. For example, tree-lined streets such as Phan Đình Phùng in Hà Nội would lose the shade that makes June bearable. As a result, more older people and outdoor workers would suffer from heatstroke. Second, people would lose their easiest place to exercise and rest. The reason is that a local park is often the only free green space where people can walk, run or sit quietly. For instance, if Central Park disappeared, New Yorkers who jog there would have only crowded pavements. This would mean more stress and less exercise for people who already spend their days indoors. In short, a city stripped of its parks and trees would be a hotter and less healthy place to live.

Now compare
  • Name the frame words that open each slot of the model.
  • Only one middle sentence has no would. Which one, and why is a present verb fine there?
  • Follow one chain from the trees in sentence 3 to the people in sentence 5.
  • Borrow two things from the model, then revise your draft on the left.
Stage 9e

Band 5 → band 7: improve the paragraph one part at a time

A student’s paragraph on a different Frame C question. The bands are the IELTS-style scale from the handbook; on our rubric, band 7 means a 3 on most criteria. Pick the band-7 version every time.
Band-5 paragraphWhat would happen if every student had to grow one plant?

If every student grow one plant, it will be very good. Students will happy. Firstly they learn about plant. Secondly school become green. Thirdly air is fresh. But some student forget water. So it is good idea.

1 · Which topic sentence would work in place of sentences 1 and 2?
D keeps the change imagined (had to … would) and promises two effects. A puts would after If and slips into will, B is an announcement, C promises nothing.
2 · Which sentence turns Firstly they learn about plant into an explained effect?
A gives the effect with would and the chain behind it (because …). B keeps the mistakes and joins two sentences with a comma, C uses you and will, D is still a list.
3 · Which example could support the effect in question 2?
C is one typical case, kept in the imagined world. A is about a friend, B is too general, D makes up a number.
4 · Which last sentence upgrades So it is good idea?
B sums up both effects in new words and keeps would. A says nothing, C adds a new idea, D slips into the real conditional.
What changed between band 5 and band 7: a topic sentence that keeps the change imagined and promises two effects · the Firstly, Secondly, Thirdly list became one effect with its chain and a typical case · will became would all through · the last sentence sums up both effects · grow, happy, plant, become corrected. (A full band-7 paragraph would also give the second effect its chain and its case.)
Stage 9f

Which peer comment helps most?

1 · Which comment would help most with a big problem (content or organisation) in the band-5 paragraph?
C names a strength, the problem, why it matters and a fix; A and B are too vague, and D picks a small point that is not the real problem.
2 · Which comment is most useful for a small language problem?
D names one error, says why it is wrong and shows the repair; the rest give the writer nothing to act on.

Last check before handing in: the Have I …? list

Organisationsentence 1 names the topic and the kind and number of points; the two points in a clear order; a last sentence that sums up or looks aheadthe topic sentence promises causes but the body gives effects (or the reverse), or the last sentence adds something newno topic sentence or no concluding sentence; causes and effects mixed upStages 1, 2, 7, 8

Vocabulary & tonethe question paraphrased; cause–effect language and topic words used precisely; a formal tonea few phrases copied from the question; two or three informal wordsa spoken style, very simple words, the question copied word for wordStages 2, 3, 4
Grammar & accuracya mix of simple and complex sentences, well controlled; Frame C keeps would for its imagined effects; errors are rarecomplex sentences tried with some errors (would after If, will in Frame C, affect / effect, lead to + verb)most sentences have errors, and the meaning is often unclearStages 2, 6, 7

Exercise 7 · The second conditional — the verb forms

Exercise 7

Choose the verb form for each gap: past simple after if, would + verb in the result

In the SB text, gaps 1 and 7 are in the if‑clause, so they take the past simple; the other gaps are results, so they take would / wouldn’t + verb (TB note). Rules: SB p. 178 · Mai Lan Hương pp. 306–307.

Part 1 · SB p. 143, Exercise 7

What would happen if there wasn’t a Gulf Stream?

The Gulf Stream is a stream of warm water which begins in Florida and travels across the Atlantic Ocean. As a result, countries on the west coast of Europe have warmer climates. If the Gulf Stream (1) (stop)if‑clause → past simple, never would flowing, Europe (2) (be)result → would + base verb very different. Countries like Great Britain (3) (become)result → would become much colder, especially in winter. If the sea was colder, spring and summer (4) (not / last)result, negative → wouldn't + base verb as long. Exercise 17 · Reading — text completion: Benjamin Franklin and the kite

Exercise 17

Read the short history and choose the best option for each gap

The text joins the two halves of the unit: lightning from 12a, a scientist answering a strange question in 12b’s spirit. Gaps 5 and 6 are a second conditional; gaps 2 and 7 are every‑ / no‑ words.

Benjamin Franklin, a kite and a key

In the 1740s, scientists still argued about what lightning really was. Benjamin Franklin, a printer from Philadelphia who now spent most of his time on science, believed that it was simply a giant spark of (1) a noun after a spark of → electricity. To test the idea, he needed something tall enough to reach the storm clouds, but there was (2) positive verb (was) + no place → nowhere, adjective after it high enough in the city.

So in June 1752, with the help of his son William, he (3) in June 1752 → past simple of fly: flew a kite made from a large silk handkerchief into a thunderstorm. A sharp, pointed wire stood up from the top of the kite, and a metal key (4) someone tied the key → past passive was tied near the bottom of the wet string, where it joined a silk ribbon. Franklin held the ribbon and stayed under a roof, so the silk kept dry. Lightning never actually struck the kite, and that was lucky: if lightning (5) an imagined case → if + past simple hit (same form as the base verb) a kite like that, the person holding the string (6) result → would + probably + passive be killed. Instead, the storm clouds slowly charged the wet string, and when Franklin moved his hand close to the key, a small spark jumped across. Lightning really was electricity. Not (7) Not everybody = some people, but not all who tried such experiments was so fortunate: in 1753 the scientist Georg Richmann was killed in St Petersburg while he was testing a metal rod during a storm.

Franklin turned his discovery into something useful: the lightning rod. It is an iron rod with a sharp point; its top rises (8) higher than the roof → above the highest part of a building, and its bottom goes deep into the damp ground. When lightning hits the rod, the electricity runs down into the earth (9) into the earth, not through the walls → instead of + noun through the walls. In September 1752 he fitted one to his own house, with two small bells that rang whenever the wire was charged. He never took out a patent on it, (10) the reason, with a full clause (he believed …) → because he believed that inventions should be shared freely.

Exercise 18 · Writing — put the cause–effect paragraph in order

Exercise 18

Give each of the ten sentences its place in the paragraph, from 1 to 10

One paragraph on Sheet 8’s Frame B (the effects of a real event): topic sentence · effect 1 · explanation · example · result · effect 2 · explanation · example · result · a concluding sentence. The first / second effect, the linkers and the words that point back (this, those, the) fix the order.
The question

What are the effects of a strong typhoon on a district hospital?

For example, if the lights go out in the middle of an operation, the team has to keep working by torchlight until the generator starts.
Because of this, the staff who are already inside often have to work two shifts in a row.
A strong typhoon has two serious effects on a district hospital, even when the building itself is not damaged.
The reason is that fallen trees and landslides block the roads for hours or even days.
The first effect is that the hospital often loses its main power supply.
In short, a typhoon can cut a hospital off from both its power and its people, even if its walls are still standing.
As a result, even a simple operation becomes slower and riskier for the patient on the table.
This happens because strong winds bring down power lines across the district, and repairs can take days.
For instance, on those blocked roads, the nurses for the next shift may be stuck in their villages.
The second effect is that patients and staff cannot reach the hospital easily.
The paragraph in order · the words that link each sentence are marked

1A strong typhoon has two serious effects on a district hospital, even when the building itself is not damaged.

1 · Topic sentence. The topic + has two serious effects on: it promises effects, not causes.

2The first effect is that the hospital often loses its main power supply.

2 · Effect 1. The first effect is that opens the first of the two effects promised in sentence 1.

3This happens because strong winds bring down power lines across the district, and repairs can take days.

3 · Explanation of effect 1. This happens because says why the power goes (sentence 2).

4For example, if the lights go out in the middle of an operation, the team has to keep working by torchlight until the generator starts.

4 · Example of effect 1. the lights picks up the power supply of sentences 2–3 and shows one real moment.

5As a result, even a simple operation becomes slower and riskier for the patient on the table.

5 · Result of the example. the patient on the table is the patient in the operation of sentence 4.

6The second effect is that patients and staff cannot reach the hospital easily.

6 · Effect 2. The second effect is that moves on to the second promised effect.

7The reason is that fallen trees and landslides block the roads for hours or even days.

7 · Explanation of effect 2. The reason is that says why nobody can get in (sentence 6).

8For instance, on those blocked roads, the nurses for the next shift may be stuck in their villages.

8 · Example of effect 2. those blocked roads are the roads of sentence 7.

9Because of this, the staff who are already inside often have to work two shifts in a row.

9 · Result of the example. the staff who are already inside are the opposite of the nurses stuck outside in sentence 8.

10In short, a typhoon can cut a hospital off from both its power and its people, even if its walls are still standing.

10 · Concluding sentence. In short sums up both effects (power and people) and adds nothing new.

Exercise 19 · Speaking — build a 7-step answer: the weekend nature trip

Exercise 19

Recommend one place for the cadets’ nature weekend: choose the sentence for each step

Situation

The academy will organise one weekend nature trip for cadets this term. Class K84 has been asked to recommend one of three places near Hà Nội.

Your class commander asks you: ‘Which place should we choose, and why?’

1🌲Ba Vì National Parkforest trails up to King Peak (1,296 m) · about 50 km west of central Hà Nội
2⛰️Tam Đảo National Parka cool, misty hill town at 930 m, built by the French in 1907 · forest walks and the Silver Waterfall · about 85 km north‑west
3🛶Vân Long Wetland Nature Reservebamboo boats between limestone hills · home of the rare Delacour’s langur · about 85 km south, in Ninh Bình
  • Choose one place
  • Give your main reason
  • Say why the other two suit one weekend less well
  • 1' prepare · 2' speak

First put the model together: for each step, choose the sentence that does that step’s job. Then close the key and give your own answer, for the same place or a different one.

Point
Point: the choice, said in one short sentence.
Why
Why: the main reason: what makes this place different (a wetland, a rare species).
How
How: the practical plan: when to leave, what to do, when to be back.
Example
Example: one real visitor and one moment on the boat.
Result
Result: what changed for that same person afterwards.
Limitation
Limitation: Admittedly …, but … is fair to the other two places, then answers them.
Evaluation
Evaluation: a final judgement from a new angle (what makes a trip worth it), not the Point again.
Model answer

PointIf we can only have one weekend, I'd go for Vân Long. WhyMainly because it's a wetland, so it'd show us a kind of nature most of us have never seen up close, and it's home to the biggest group of Delacour's langurs left anywhere in the world. HowWe could leave the academy early on Saturday, spend the morning on the bamboo boats that local people row between the limestone hills, and still be back by Sunday lunchtime. ExampleMy cousin went there with her biology class last spring, and from the boat she spotted two langurs sitting on a cliff above the water. ResultShe's been back twice since then with a zoom lens, and now she wants to write her final-year project on the reserve. LimitationAdmittedly, Ba Vì is closer and Tam Đảo is cooler, but plenty of us have hiked in Ba Vì already, and Tam Đảo gets so crowded at weekends that you'd hardly notice any wildlife. EvaluationOn balance, a trip like this is only worth it if it shows us something new, and Vân Long would do that better than anywhere else on the list.

2:00

Exercise 20 · Writing — complete a “What if …?” answer: the bees

Exercise 20

Complete the blog answer: choose the best option for each gap

An answer in the style of Randall’s blog: a strange question, a scientific answer. Gaps 2, 3, 5, 7, 8 and 9 are the second conditional; gaps 1, 4, 6 and 10 are every‑ / some‑ / no‑ / any‑ words. Homework (Day 7 of the 1‑3‑7 plan, Sheet 10): your own 120–150‑word answer to What would happen if it never rained in Hà Nội in summer?

What would happen if all the bees disappeared?

A reader asks: My grandfather keeps bees. He says that if bees disappeared, humans would die out in four years. Is that true?

Not quite. That warning is often linked to Albert Einstein, but nobody has ever found (1) nobody is already negative → any; nobody … no would be a double negative record of him saying it. Still, if every bee on Earth (2) an imagined situation → if + past simple disappeared tomorrow, our lives (3) result → would + base verb a lot.

Bees carry pollen from flower to flower, and many crops can’t make fruit unless (4) a thing we don’t name (an insect, a bird, the wind) → something moves that pollen for them. Rice, wheat and maize (5) result, negative → wouldn’t be in much danger, because they don’t need insects to make their grain. Apples, almonds and melons, on the other hand, would become much harder to grow. Other insects, birds and bats also carry pollen, so fruit wouldn’t vanish completely, but there would be far less of it. (6) all the shoppers → Everybody + singular would notice would notice the difference at the market, because fruit, vegetables and nuts (7) result → would cost much more.

Doctors would worry too. A 2015 study in The Lancet estimated that if all animal pollinators, not only bees, (8) if‑clause → past simple vanished, about 1.4 million more people (9) result → would die every year from heart disease, stroke and other illnesses linked to a poor diet. In Hanyuan, a pear‑growing county in Sichuan, China, farmers already pollinate their trees by hand, touching each flower with a stick tipped with chicken feathers. If bees disappeared (10) in all places, all over the world → everywhere, far more farmers would have to do this slow, tiring work.

So no, humans wouldn’t die out in four years. But our plates would be much less colourful, and our doctors would be a lot busier.

16-chunk quiz

Quiz

Write the chunk for each meaning: the brackets show how it is built, and other correct forms also count

1electricity from a storm cloud that you see as a flash (one noun, no e after the t)
lightning: uncountable; lightening means making something lighter
2be struck by that flash from the sky (be + past participle + by + noun)
be hit by lightning: no a before lightning; struck by works too
3a message telling people that a river may soon cover the land (a + noun + noun)
a flood warning: noun + noun, like a storm warning
4look at what the weather is going to do (verb + the + noun + noun)
check the weather forecast; then the forecast says …
5go the other way, away from the danger (verb + in + the + adjective + noun)
in the opposite direction: the preposition is in, not to
6temperatures below zero degrees (adjective + noun)
freezing = below 0 °C; frozen = already turned to ice
7faster than any passenger plane flies today (at + the + noun + of + noun)
at the speed of sound: at + a speed
8a situation that will probably never happen (an + adjective + noun)
unlikely = probably won’t happen; impossible = can’t happen
9the start of a piece of advice (If + I + … + you)
If I were you, I’d … + base verb; were for every person (was in speech)
10the question about an imagined situation (What + would + you + verb + if)
What would you do if + past simple …? Never would after if.
11a green place near your home where people walk their dogs (a + adjective + noun)
a local park = one near where you live
12a very long way from cities and villages (far away from + any + plural noun)
far (away) from any + plural noun: any, because the meaning is negative
13land where the law stops people hunting or building (a + adjective + noun)
a protected area: protect → protected (the law protects it)
14the space inside a box with every side 30.5 centimetres long (one + adjective + noun)
one cubic foot: one foot ≈ 30.5 cm; one foot, two feet
15all the different kinds of living things that grow or move (noun + of + noun + and + noun)
species: the same form for one and for many
16see and pay attention to the animals close to you (verb + the + noun + around + you)
notice = see and pay attention; wildlife has no plural

1b
Past simple or would?
3′

Pick the verb form for each gap, then press Check: the if clause and the would clause need different forms.

1If lightning the old banyan tree, half the town would hear the crack.
This is the if clause of an imagined situation, so the past simple: hit. Would never goes after if.
2If it snowed in Huế, the old citadel like a Christmas card.
The result clause takes would + base verb: would look.
3We boats to reach the clinic if the river flooded tonight.
The result clause comes first here, but it still needs would; with if in the middle there is no comma.
4If I in charge of the duty roster, I’d keep a medic at the gate on every stormy night.
If clause: past form of be. Were is correct for every person (was is common in speech).
5Where would you go if the power off during the night shift?
The question is in the would clause (Where would you go); the if clause needs the past simple: went.
6If the forecast hail, the farmers would cover their fruit trees.
Past simple after if; the farmers’ reaction is in the would clause.
7The hospital its patients upstairs if the ground floor flooded.
The result of the imagined flood: would move. The past simple belongs to the if clause (flooded).
8If you under a lone tree in a thunderstorm, you wouldn’t be safe.
If clause, past simple of stand: stood.
9If we had a weather radio in the dormitory, we warnings much sooner.
had is already in the if clause, so the second half needs would: would hear.
10Flying the rescue helicopter impossible if the wind reached 150 km/h.
The imagined result goes in the would clause: would be impossible.

Pairs that look alike
