GoalChoose between weather and “What if …?” words that look or sound alike, and give a reason for each choice.
2a
Compare the pairs
8′

Read both sides of every card. Then cover them, tap the quick test and answer it.

thunder · lightning
thunder /ˈθʌndə(r)/
the part of a storm your ears catch: crashes and rumbles you never see
The thunder was so loud that the windows in our classroom shook.
lightning /ˈlaɪtnɪŋ/
the part your eyes catch: a jagged white line that is gone in under a second
Every few seconds, a flash of lightning turned the night sky purple.
✗ I couldn’t sleep because the lightning was so loud. (→ thunder)
lightning · lightening
lightning /ˈlaɪtnɪŋ/
the storm word: nine letters, l‑i‑g‑h‑t‑n‑i‑n‑g
The tall pine by the gate has a black scar where lightning struck it.
lightening /ˈlaɪtnɪŋ/
from the verb lighten: becoming lighter in colour or in weight; it sounds the same
The sky was lightening in the east as we set off on the morning run.
✗ The storm brought lightening and strong winds. (→ lightning)
a storm · a thunderstorm · a typhoon
a storm /ə stɔːm/
the general word: wind, rain or snow rough enough to keep you indoors
A storm kept the supply boat in harbour for three days.
a thunderstorm /ə ˈθʌndəstɔːm/
one that brings thunder and lightning; often over within an hour
The afternoon thunderstorm lasted forty minutes and turned the car park into a lake.
a typhoon /ə taɪˈfuːn/
the strongest kind to reach Vietnam from the Pacific, with winds that can rip off roofs
The typhoon brought down power lines all along the coast.
✗ Last night’s typhoon was just ten minutes of thunder over the academy. (→ thunderstorm)
a flood · a drought
a flood /ə flʌd/
too much water covering land that is usually dry
After the flood, the clinic floor was covered in ten centimetres of mud.
a drought /ə draʊt/
the opposite problem: month after month without rain
The drought went on so long that the village well ran dry.
✗ The rice died in the flood, because no rain fell for five months. (→ drought)
damage · injure
damage /ˈdæmɪdʒ/
used for things: a roof, a car, a crop
The storm damaged the roof of the sports hall and flattened the vegetable garden.
injure /ˈɪndʒə(r)/
used for bodies: a person or an animal gets hurt
Two soldiers were injured when the wind blew a tent pole over.
✗ Flying glass damaged the driver’s hand. (→ injured)
safe · safety
safe /seɪf/
adjective: out of danger (a safe place, stay safe)
The basement is the safest place in the building during a typhoon.
safety /ˈseɪfti/
noun: the idea of avoiding accidents (fire safety, for your safety)
The lifeguards closed the beach for our safety until the warning was lifted.
✗ The captain checked that everyone was safety before he left the bunker. (→ safe)
unlikely · impossible
unlikely /ʌnˈlaɪkli/
a small chance, but still a chance
It’s unlikely to snow in Sa Pa this winter, but it isn’t out of the question.
impossible /ɪmˈpɒsəbl/
zero chance: nobody could ever do it
It’s impossible for a person to run at the speed of sound.
✗ Snow in Sa Pa is impossible, although it fell there in January 2016. (→ unlikely)
If it rains, we’ll … · If it snowed, we’d …
If + present, will
a real situation that may well happen (first conditional)
If it rains tomorrow, we’ll hold the first-aid class in the gym.
If + past, would
an imagined situation that is unlikely or impossible now (second conditional)
If it snowed on Ba Vì tomorrow, half the academy would want to go and see it.
✗ If the typhoon comes tonight, we would move the patients upstairs. (→ we’ll move: the typhoon is forecast, so it is real)
2b
Which one, and why?
7′
1 · Count the seconds after the flash: if the ____ comes almost at once, the storm is right above you.
thunder: the sound that follows the flash. Lightning is the flash itself, and lightening means getting lighter.
2 · The rice fields were cracked and brown after months of ____.
drought: cracked, dry land means too little water. A flood or storms would bring too much.
3 · My grandmother says the hailstorm of 1998 ____ every roof in her village.
damaged: roofs are things. We injure or hurt people and animals.
4 · If I ____ you, I wouldn’t drive across that flooded bridge.
were: If I were you is the fixed way to give advice with the second conditional.
5 · Please read the fire ____ rules on the back of your door.
safety: a noun that describes the rules, like road safety. Safe is an adjective, safely an adverb.
6 · Swimming across the Pacific in a week is ____.
impossible: nobody could do it at all. Unlikely leaves a small chance, and unpredictable means you can’t say what will happen.
7 · If a typhoon ____ the academy tomorrow, the exams would be moved.
hit: the other clause has would, so the if clause needs the past simple. Hits would need will in the other half.
8 · The ____ for tomorrow is sunshine in the morning and thunderstorms after 3 p.m.
forecast: a report of the weather that is coming. A warning is only about danger, and the climate is the usual weather over many years.
Step 3 / 6 · Control

Choose and correct

Active · with help⏱ 10 min
GoalUse the weather words and the second conditional accurately, and correct sentences that get them wrong.
3a
Fix the sentence
5′

The underlined part of each sentence is wrong. Choose the correct version from the list.

1If lightning would strike the flagpole during drill, everyone on the parade ground would jump.
→
The if clause of an imagined situation takes the past simple, never would: struck. (Stroke is another word: the illness, or a verb meaning “touch gently”.)
2Our tent was only twenty metres from where the lightening came down.
→
The flash in the sky is lightning, with no e; it is uncountable, so no a and no ‑s.
3The typhoon did a lot of damages to the rice fields near my home.
→
Damage to things is uncountable: a lot of damage. Injuries are to people.
4If I will be the captain, I’d cancel tonight’s march because of the storm.
→
An imagined situation (I am not the captain): If I were …, I’d … Never will or would after if.
5Hails as big as eggs dented every car in the car park.
→
Hail is uncountable; to count the pieces, use hailstones.
6If my village had a proper flood wall, my parents won’t worry every rainy season.
→
had in the if clause shows an imagined situation, so the result needs wouldn’t, not won’t.
7It’s unlike that the river will flood again this year; the bank has been rebuilt.
→
The adjective is unlikely (there is only a small chance). Unlike is a preposition: unlike my brother, I love storms.
8The whether forecast says heavy rain all weekend.
→
Weather = rain, sun, wind. Whether sounds the same but means if: I don’t know whether it will rain.
9Where you would shelter if a tornado came straight towards your car?
→
In a question, would goes before the subject: Where would you shelter if …?
10Falling branches damaged three cadets who were running back to the barracks.
→
People are injured; things are damaged.
3b
Complete Lan’s answer on the class “What if …?” board
5′

Q: What would happen if a hailstorm hit the academy during the morning parade?

If a hailstorm (1) the if clause of an imagined situation: past simple, never would the academy during the morning parade, nobody (2) the result clause: would + base verb in line for long. Hailstones the size of marbles really hurt, so the officers would send us running for the nearest roof, and the band would probably save their trumpets before their heads! The ice would cause some (3) damage to things is uncountable: some damage to the cars by the main gate, too. Of course, (4) the subject of the sentence must be a noun: safety would come first, and the medical team would check anyone with cuts on their hands or face. A hailstorm on a parade morning isn’t impossible, but it’s very (5) isn’t impossible, but points to a small chance: unlikely in Hà Nội, which is why nobody brings a helmet just in case. If it ever (6) another if clause, matched with I’d in the result: past simple, though, I’d grab my phone and film the whole thing from the library steps.

Step 5 / 6 · Produce

Speak, upgrade, then try a new task

Active · freely⏱ 18 min
GoalGive a 20-second answer to a “What if …?” weather question, upgrade it with the 7-step frame, then answer a child’s science question.
5a
Upgrade my answer
8′
Speaking task · a 20-second “What if …?” answer

‘What would you do if a typhoon warning came during exam week?’

Talk for about 20 seconds with Tier 1 words: what you would do first, what you would prepare and how you would feel.

Example

First I’d check the weather forecast to see when the typhoon was due. Then I’d charge my phone, fill a few bottles with water and move my notes away from the window. I’d keep revising, of course, but to be honest I’d be thinking more about the storm than the exam.

Now say it through the 7-step frame, adding two Tier 2 chunks; keep each step to one short sentence.

Example

PointIf a typhoon warning came in the middle of exam week, I’d treat the storm as the more serious test. WhyExams can be moved to another day, but a smashed window or a flooded room takes weeks to put right. HowI’d keep checking the weather forecast, charge everything I own and put my books on the top shelf. ExampleTwo years ago a storm knocked out the power in my hometown three days before my school-leaving exams. ResultBecause my mum had bought candles and filled every bottle the day before, I lost hardly any revision time. LimitationIn theory, the academy might call off the exams anyway, and all that planning would look a bit silly. EvaluationStill, I’d rather be ready for nothing than caught out by something.

Choose one follow-up question and answer it in about 20 seconds.

  • Should the academy move exams online whenever a storm warning comes?
  • What would you put in a typhoon bag for your room?
Example

I’d pack a torch, a power bank, two litres of water, some dry biscuits and a small first-aid kit. As future doctors, we’d probably be the ones the neighbours knock on the door for, so the first-aid kit would matter most.

Read the model and find each of the seven steps.

PointIf a typhoon warning came during exam week, I wouldn’t panic, but I’d change my plans that same evening. WhyThe main reason is that a strong typhoon can cause serious damage in a few hours, whereas the exam will still be there when the sky clears. HowI’d revise in the morning, get the room ready in the afternoon and keep the radio on for news of the storm’s path. ExampleTake my cousin, a pharmacy student in Huế, who got a typhoon warning the night before her biggest exam last October. ResultShe carried her motorbike and her books upstairs and slept at a friend’s house away from the river, and as a result she still walked into the exam room on time and dry. LimitationAdmittedly, it’s unlikely that the academy would cancel exams for every warning, so we might have to sit them with the wind howling outside. EvaluationEven so, if I were in that situation, I’d sort out the room first and the notes second, because you can resit a paper, but you can’t dry out a flooded laptop overnight.

Hide the model and answer the question again in 60–90 seconds, going through all seven steps.

5b
New situation · answer a child’s “What if …?” question
10′
Task · spoken answer · 45–60 seconds

At the academy’s open day, a ten-year-old visitor asks you: ‘What would happen if lightning hit our school bus?’ These are the notes on the weather-safety leaflet in your pocket.

  • lightning / usually hits / the tallest thing nearby
  • bus with a metal roof and sides / electricity / runs through the metal body / into the ground
  • rubber tyres / NOT the reason you are safe
  • inside: windows closed · hands off metal parts · wait until the storm passes
  • outside: open fields, hilltops, under a lone tree / the worst places
  1. Answer the question with If lightning hit …, … would … and give the scientific reason.
  2. Add one safety tip with If I were you, I’d …
1:00Tap every chunk you use.
🚀 Challenge card

Do at least two:

  • use if + past simple and would at least twice
  • give the scientific reason with because or so
  • use one Tier 2 chunk (be hit by lightning, in theory, an unlikely situation)
  • add the opposite case: what would happen if the child were outside
Suggested answers · 3 levels
● Core

The answerThat’s a great question! If lightning hit your school bus, you would be safe inside. The electricity would go through the metal of the bus and down into the ground. It wouldn’t go through you.

A safety tipIf I were you, I’d stay in my seat and keep my hands in my lap until the storm stopped. And please don’t touch the metal door!

●● Stretch

The answerIn theory, a bus is one of the best places to be in a thunderstorm. If it was hit by lightning, the electricity would race across the outside of the bus and then down to the ground. You’d hear a terrible bang, but you’d be fine. Lots of people think the rubber tyres protect you, but it’s really the metal body.

A safety tipIf I were you, I’d keep the windows shut and sit tight. The really dangerous place would be the football field outside.

●●● Challenge

The answerIt sounds scary, but it’s an unlikely situation to get hurt in. Lightning usually goes for the tallest thing around, so if it hit your bus, the electricity would flow over the metal shell and into the ground, a bit like rain running off an umbrella. The bus might need a new aerial, but the children inside would almost certainly be fine.

A safety tipNow, if you were standing in an open field instead, it would be a very different story, because you’d be the tallest thing there. So if I were you, I’d run for the bus at the first rumble of thunder, shut the windows and keep your hands off anything metal.

Pick the word that fits each sentence, then press Check. Look at the verb first: is it negative, a question, an offer?

1I looked under every rock by the pond, but I didn’t find .
The verb is already negative (didn’t), so anything; nothing would make a double negative.
2 in my room has a phone, so we can all use the plant app.
we can all = all the people: Everyone, with a singular verb (has).
3All the benches are wet, so there’s to sit.
There’s is a positive verb with a negative meaning: nowhere. Anywhere would need there isn’t.
4Would you like to drink after the walk?

5 saw the snake except the guide.

6Did take a photo of the kingfisher?

7There were mosquitoes near the lake, so bring some cream next time.

8Could help me carry the frame down to the stream?

9We heard moving in the long grass, but we couldn’t see what it was.
A positive verb and a thing we can’t name: something.
10I’m tired of the same paths; let’s find this weekend.
The adjective comes after the pronoun: somewhere new, something green.

The guide pointed out four species of butterfly in the first ten minutes of the walk.

notice /ˈnəʊtɪs/

I’d walked past the guardhouse a hundred times before I noticed the tiny ferns growing out of its roof.

Check questions
✓ notice the ferns✗ notice to the ferns
nearby /ˌnɪəˈbaɪ/

There’s a small wetland nearby, just ten minutes’ walk from the north gate.

Check questions

Flash cards · say the missing word, then tap the card to see if you were right.

Step 2 / 6 · Tell apart

Pairs that look alike

Passive → active⏱ 15 min
GoalTell apart nature words and every-, some-, no-, any- words that are easy to confuse, and explain your choice.
2a
Compare the pairs
8′

Read both sides of every card. Then cover them, tap the quick test and answer it.

nature · the nature of …
nature /ˈneɪtʃə(r)/
the living world outside: trees, birds, rivers, weather; no article
Two days in the hills reminded us how much we miss nature in the city.
the nature of … /ðə ˈneɪtʃər əv/
the basic character or type of something
The surgeon explained the nature of the injury before the operation.
✗ My roommate and I both love the nature, so we joined the Green Club. (→ love nature)
wildlife · a wild life
wildlife /ˈwaɪldlaɪf/
one word, uncountable: animals, birds and insects living free
The pond behind the medical library is full of wildlife after the rains.
a wild life /ə ˌwaɪld ˈlaɪf/
two words: an exciting, crazy way of living
My uncle lived a wild life as a sailor before he settled down as a teacher.
✗ The national park protects the wild life of the whole valley. (→ wildlife)
a species · two species
a species /ə ˈspiːʃiːz/
one type of plant or animal; the word ends in ‑s even in the singular
The giant water bug is a species my roommate had never seen before.
species (plural) /ˈspiːʃiːz/
several types: the same form, no ‑es
We found eleven species of plant on one square metre of the football pitch.
✗ In our first botany class we learned the names of thirty specieses. (→ species)
a frame · a cube
a frame /ə freɪm/
the edges only, around a picture, a window or an empty space
My grandfather hung my high-school graduation photo in a gold frame above the TV.
a cube /ə kjuːb/ · cubic
a solid box shape with every side the same square (an ice cube, a stock cube)
She dropped two ice cubes into my glass of lemon tea.
✗ Put your passport photo in the little cube on the desk. (→ frame)
notice · watch
notice /ˈnəʊtɪs/
suddenly see or become aware of something
Halfway through the lecture, I noticed a gecko on the ceiling.
watch /wɒtʃ/
look at something for some time, often as it moves or changes
We watched the ants carry crumbs back to their nest for twenty minutes.
✗ Did you watch that the river was much higher today? (→ notice)
natural · man-made
natural /ˈnætʃrəl/
there before humans came, like a mountain, a river or a cave
Hạ Long Bay, with its limestone islands, is one of Vietnam’s great natural wonders.
man-made /ˌmæn ˈmeɪd/
there because someone dug, planted or built it
The football pitch, the canal and the rice terraces are all man-made.
✗ A rice field is a natural place because it’s green. (→ man-made: farmers made it)
a park · a garden
a park /ə pɑːk/
green space that belongs to the city, free for anyone to use
On Sunday mornings the park by the lake fills with people doing tai chi.
a garden /ə ˈɡɑːdn/
green space that belongs to a family home (or a planned plant collection: a botanical garden)
My grandmother grows chillies and lemongrass in the garden behind her house.
✗ Hundreds of people jog in the public garden in the city centre every morning. (→ park)
something · anything · nothing
something /ˈsʌmθɪŋ/
a thing we can’t or don’t name; positive sentences, offers and requests
Something scratches inside the drainpipe every night, but we’ve never seen it.
anything /ˈeniθɪŋ/
with a negative verb or in a general question
Have you seen anything unusual by the river this week?
nothing /ˈnʌθɪŋ/
no thing at all; it takes a positive verb
We waited an hour by the nest, but nothing came out.
✗ I didn’t photograph nothing all morning. (→ anything, or: I photographed nothing)
2b
Which one, and why?
7′
1 · Herons, frogs and dragonflies: the lake behind the hospital is full of ____.
wildlife: one word for animals living free. A wild life is an exciting way of living.
2 · ____ in the class knew the name of the tiny blue flower, not even the teacher.
Nobody: not even the teacher shows the meaning is “no person”, and the verb knew is positive. Anybody would need didn’t know.
3 · I counted at least nine ____ of bird on our morning run.
species: the plural has the same form as the singular.
4 · The ____ around the photo was made of old bamboo.
frame: the border around a picture. A cube is a solid shape, and cubic is an adjective.
5 · Is there ____ in the city where you can hear frogs at night instead of traffic?
anywhere: a general question about a place. Nowhere doesn’t fit a question like this, and everywhere would mean all places.
6 · I only ____ the tiny frog on my boot when it jumped onto my hand.
noticed: I suddenly became aware of it. Watch lasts for some time, and look needs at.
7 · We spend so much time indoors that many of us feel cut off from ____.
nature: in general, with no article and no plural.
8 · Everybody in my study group ____ a different favourite animal.
has: everybody means all the people, but it takes a singular verb.
Step 3 / 6 · Control

Choose and correct

Active · with help⏱ 10 min
GoalUse the nature words and the every-, some-, no-, any- words accurately, and correct the sentences that misuse them.
3a
Fix the sentence
5′

The underlined part of each sentence is wrong. Choose the correct version from the list.

1On Sundays I try to spend an hour in the nature, even if it’s only the academy garden.
→
Nature in general takes no article: spend time in nature.
2Everybody I know have a favourite spot for watching the sunset.
→
Everybody takes a singular verb: everybody has.
3We searched the riverbank all morning but didn’t spot nothing unusual.
→
didn’t is already negative, so anything; two negatives in one clause are wrong.
4I’d like to go quiet somewhere this weekend, away from the traffic.
→
The adjective goes after the pronoun: somewhere quiet.
5Our biology club found three specieses of beetle under one log.
→
The plural of species is species: no ‑es.
6Noone noticed the frog until it jumped onto the map.
→
No one is two words (but nobody, nothing and nowhere are one).
7The academy garden is full of wild life if you sit still for ten minutes.
→
Animals living free: wildlife, one word and uncountable.
8I’ve photographed the lotus pond; now I want to try else somewhere.
→
Else comes after the pronoun: somewhere else, nothing else.
9Each green frame is measured exactly one foot along every edge.
→
To give a size, measure is active and in the present simple: each frame measures …
10Last night I took a photo to a moth sitting on my mosquito net.
→
The collocation is take a photo of something.
3b
Complete Minh’s post for the Green Club board
5′

One cubic foot, one week

Last Monday our platoon put a green frame (1) a positive sentence and a place we don’t need to name: somewhere (+ the adjective after it) quiet behind the canteen, under the old almond tree. At first we thought there was (2) there was is positive, and the meaning is “no thing”: nothing there except dry leaves and an old plastic bag. Then, on Tuesday, Hùng spotted two tiny (3) two + a regular plural: insects, each one smaller than one millimetre, walking along a leaf. By Friday we had counted eleven (4) the plural of species keeps the same form of plants and animals. (5) all the people, with a singular verb (checks): Everybody in the platoon now checks the frame after lunch. Have you found (6) a general question: anything (+ the adjective after it) interesting near your building? Tell us at the Saturday meeting!

middle of Hà Nội · no forest · but · find · nature · every street · if · look closely

Make it true for you
5′

Complete each frame so it is true about your life, with at least one Tier 2 chunk. Then read the two examples.

Somewhere near my dormitory, …

Examples

1Somewhere near my dormitory, a pair of bulbuls has built a nest in the hedge, and you can hear the chicks every morning at six.

2Somewhere near my dormitory, there’s a corner of the sports field that nobody mows, and it’s full of wild flowers and butterflies.

If I had a green frame for one week, I’d put it … because …

Examples

1If I had a green frame for one week, I’d put it half in and half out of the fish pond in the botany garden, because I’d get water life and land life in the same cube.

2If I had a green frame for one week, I’d put it on the flat roof of our building, because I’m curious whether anything at all lives up there.

Nobody in my family …, but everybody …

Examples

1Nobody in my family likes snakes, but everybody stops to watch the swallows when they come back in spring.

2Nobody in my family has ever been to a national park, but everybody knows the name of every plant in my grandmother’s garden.

Step 5 / 6 · Produce

Speak, upgrade, then try a new task

Active · freely⏱ 18 min
GoalDescribe one cubic foot of nature near your dormitory with the 7-step frame, then present your platoon’s frame and write its notice.
5a
Upgrade my answer
8′
Speaking task · a 20-second description

‘Describe one cubic foot of nature near your dormitory. Use at least three words that begin with every-, some-, no- or any-.’

Talk for about 20 seconds with Tier 1 words: where the spot is, what lives there and why nobody notices it.

Example

Right outside my dormitory there’s a patch of grass under a mango tree. At first it looks like nothing special, but there’s always something moving if you look closely: ants, a little spider, sometimes a snail after rain. Nobody else ever stops there, so it feels like my own secret garden.

Now say it through the 7-step frame, adding two Tier 2 chunks; keep each step to one short sentence.

Example

PointThe cubic foot I’d pick is the drain cover by the canteen, where moss grows round the edges. WhyEveryone walks past it, and nobody ever looks down. HowI sometimes crouch there with my phone and take a photo of whatever is moving. ExampleAfter the rain last week, a frog no bigger than my thumbnail sat on it all morning while two cadets nearly trod on it. ResultSince I told my platoon, half of them look down every time they pass. LimitationIn the dry season, though, there’s nothing much to see apart from dust. EvaluationStill, it showed me that you can find nature without ever going out of the gate.

Choose one follow-up question and answer it in about 20 seconds.

  • Would you rather photograph wildlife in a national park or in your own street? Why?
  • Should the academy leave one corner of the campus completely wild?
Example

Yes, I think so. If one corner were left alone, it would fill up with insects and birds within a year, and our biology lecturers could teach out there instead of from slides.

Read the model and find each of the seven steps.

PointIf I had David Liittschwager’s green frame for a week, I’d put it in the narrow strip of grass between our dormitory and the bike shed, a spot that nobody thinks of as nature. WhyThe reason is that I’m sure there’s something alive in every corner of the campus, even where it looks bare. HowI’d check the frame twice a day, before drill and after dinner, and take a photo of everything that moved or grew inside it. ExampleFor example, when I sat there with a torch one evening last week, I counted two kinds of beetle, a centipede and a snail working its way up a blade of grass. ResultAs a result, my roommates now call that patch ‘the zoo’, and two of them have started checking it too. LimitationAdmittedly, a cubic foot of grass in Hà Nội can’t compete with a coral reef for colour, and some days there’s nothing to see but ants. EvaluationEven so, I’d rather show people the wildlife under their own windows, because that’s the nature they could actually protect.

Hide the model and describe your cubic foot again in 60 seconds, moving through all seven steps.

5b
New situation · One Cubic Foot Week
10′
Task · speak and write

The academy’s Green Club is running “One Cubic Foot Week”: each platoon puts a frame somewhere on the campus for five days and reports what lives inside it. You are the one who will present your platoon’s choice.

  1. Speak · 45 seconds: say where your platoon would put its frame, what you expect to find there and why you chose that spot.
  2. Write · 3 minutes: the notice for your platoon’s board, 4–5 sentences, with one any- question and one sentence with every- or no-.
0:45Tap every chunk you use.
🚀 Challenge card

Do at least two:

  • use the second conditional once (If we put …, we’d …)
  • put an adjective or else after a pronoun (somewhere damp, nothing else)
  • use one Tier 2 chunk (notice the wildlife around you, species of plants and animals)
  • end your notice with a question that starts Has anyone …? or Is there anything …?
Suggested answers · 3 levels
● Core

Our spotWe want to put our frame under the big tree next to the canteen. There are always leaves and insects there. I think we will find ants, spiders and maybe a frog.

Our noticeOne Cubic Foot Week starts on Monday! Our frame is under the tree next to the canteen. Everyone can visit it after lunch. Please don’t move anything inside the frame. Does anyone have a good camera?

●● Stretch

Our spotIf we put our frame by the pond behind the library, we’d find life in the water and on land at the same time. Somewhere in that wet mud there must be frogs, snails and water insects, and nobody has ever looked closely.

Our noticePlatoon 3’s frame is now at the pond behind the library. Everybody is welcome to come and look, but please stay on the path. We’ve already found four species of plants and animals, and it’s only Tuesday! Has anyone got a magnifying glass we could borrow?

●●● Challenge

Our spotOur platoon has gone for the least exciting spot on the campus: the gravel strip beside the car park. Everyone told us there’d be nothing there, which is exactly why we chose it. If we found even five species in a place that looks completely dead, we’d prove that nature really is everywhere.

Our noticePlatoon 3 has put its frame somewhere nobody expected: the gravel beside the car park. In two days we have recorded seven species, including a mite smaller than one millimetre. Please walk round the frame, not through it. Is there anywhere else on the campus that you think is completely empty? Tell us, and we’ll test it next week!
